instruments.issuer: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions
instruments.name: Guideline B-10: Third-Party Risk Management Guideline
instruments.summary: Holds a federally regulated institution accountable for every third-party arrangement and expects an enterprise-wide framework covering risk and criticality assessment, due diligence, written agreements with audit, information, incident-notification and termination rights, visibility of subcontractors, concentration risk, technology and cyber standards for higher-risk providers (with specific attention to cloud and portability), ongoing monitoring, and tested exit and contingency plans for critical arrangements. It took effect on 1 May 2024 and was extended to foreign branches by a February 2024 amendment with adherence by 31 March 2025. Status caveat: OSFI published a targeted amendment on 19 November 2026, effective immediately, clarifying how the guideline applies to data sharing under the federal consumer-driven banking framework (institutions may rely on government accreditation of participants but keep responsibility for residual risks such as data integrity and cyber risk); the guideline page was modified the same day, one day before this verification, so the amended text should be re-read at the next review.
instruments.version: April 2023, as amended February 2024 (foreign branches) and 19 November 2026 (consumer-driven banking)

instruments.issuer: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions
instruments.name: Guideline B-13: Technology and Cyber Risk Management
instruments.summary: Sets OSFI's expectations in three areas: governance of technology and cyber risk (accountability, strategy, risk framework and appetite); technology operations and resilience (architecture, asset inventory, change and project management, secure development, patching, incident and problem management, disaster recovery); and cyber security (identifying threats, layered defences, detection and logging, response and recovery, including incidents at third parties). Technology bought from vendors is expected to fit within these controls. The guideline took effect on 1 January 2024; the only amendment found is the February 2024 clarification for foreign branches, and no revision or consultation was shown on OSFI's page on the verification date. A July 2026 OSFI technology risk bulletin on generative and agentic AI maps suggested practices to B-13 without amending it.

instruments.issuer: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions
instruments.name: Guideline E-21: Operational Risk Management and Resilience
instruments.summary: Expects an institution to identify its critical operations, map the people, systems and third parties they depend on, set tolerances for disruption, and test with severe but plausible scenarios (cyber incidents and third-party failures among them) whether it can stay within those tolerances, alongside a governed operational risk framework and sound business continuity, crisis, change and data risk management. For technology buying this means a vendor supporting a critical operation has to be mapped and included in resilience testing. Implementation was staged: sections 1 and 2 applied on publication (22 August 2024), section 4 from 1 September 2025, and full adherence from 1 September 2026, so the guideline now applies in full; one milestone remains, completion of scenario testing for all critical operations by 1 September 2027. OSFI's letter says the operational risk expectations have been in place since 2016, but neither it nor the guideline page names a document that E-21 replaces; OSFI's page showed no later revision on the verification date.

instruments.issuer: Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions
instruments.name: Guideline E-23 - Model Risk Management (2027)
instruments.summary: Status caveat first: this record describes the final revised Guideline E-23, published 11 September 2025, which takes effect for all federally regulated financial institutions on 1 May 2027; until then the 2017 Guideline E-23 (Enterprise-Wide Model Risk Management for Deposit-Taking Institutions) is still the version on OSFI's site, although its page does not state a status. The revised guideline expects enterprise-wide model risk management proportionate to risk: a current inventory of models with non-negligible risk, risk ratings that drive the intensity of review, and controls across the whole life cycle from design and data through independent review, deployment, monitoring and decommissioning. It applies explicitly to AI and machine-learning models (explainability, bias, drift, autonomous behaviour) and to vendor and other third-party models, which must be inventoried, rated and reviewed like internal ones, consistent with Guideline B-10.

instruments.name: CRI Profile
instruments.summary: A financial-sector cybersecurity assessment framework maintained by the Cyber Risk Institute, built around diagnostic statements that are mapped to regulatory sources and industry standards. It matters to a bank because it is designed for financial institutions and can structure both internal assessment and questions to vendors. The current version is v2.2, released on 30 April 2026; according to CRI it added 13 mappings and revised three (40 in total) without changing the core diagnostic statements. Earlier releases were v2.0 (February 2024, aligned to NIST CSF 2.0) and v2.1 (2025).

instruments.name: CSA STAR (Security, Trust, Assurance and Risk) program
instruments.summary: The Cloud Security Alliance's assurance program for cloud services, with Level 1 as a self-assessment questionnaire and Level 2 as a third-party audit that pairs the questionnaire with ISO/IEC 27001 certification or a SOC 2 attestation. It gives a bank a cloud-specific control set to compare vendors against, but a Level 1 entry is a vendor's own statement. The underlying Cloud Controls Matrix and CAIQ are at v4.1, released on 27 January 2026 (the date recorded here), so older entries may rest on an earlier version. CSA has also added a separate STAR for AI track based on its AI Controls Matrix, with Level 2 now available.
instruments.version: Based on Cloud Controls Matrix and CAIQ v4.1

instruments.issuer: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
instruments.name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act)
instruments.summary: The AI Act sets risk-based obligations for providers and deployers of AI systems, so a bank using AI in a high-risk use case, or buying such a system, takes on duties around oversight, logging, documentation and use in line with the provider's instructions, while suppliers carry provider duties. It entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies in stages: prohibited practices and AI literacy from 2 February 2025, governance and general-purpose AI model obligations from 2 August 2025, and general application from 2 August 2026. An amending regulation, (EU) 2026/1744, entered into force on 27 July 2026 and, according to the European Commission, moved the high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 for Annex III use cases and 2 August 2028 for AI embedded in Annex I regulated products. The EUR-Lex dates panel for the original act still showed the pre-amendment staging on the verification date, so the amended dates here rest on the Commission's page and the EUR-Lex record that Article 113 was changed.
instruments.version: As amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (in force 27 July 2026)

instruments.issuer: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
instruments.name: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience for the financial sector (DORA)
instruments.summary: DORA requires EU financial entities to run an ICT risk management framework, report major ICT incidents, test their digital resilience, and manage ICT third-party risk through due diligence, mandatory contract terms, a register of ICT arrangements and exit planning; it also creates EU-level oversight of ICT providers designated as critical. It entered into force on 16 January 2023 and has applied since 17 January 2025. EUR-Lex showed it as in force on the verification date, corrected in some language versions and completed by a series of delegated and implementing regulations, with no act amending the regulation itself.
instruments.version: OJ L 333, 27.12.2022; no amending acts listed on EUR-Lex (supplemented by delegated and implementing acts)

instruments.name: Guidelines on ICT and security risk management (EBA/GL/2019/04), as amended by EBA/GL/2025/02
instruments.summary: These guidelines used to set the EBA's broad expectations for ICT and security risk management at banks and payment service providers, but they were cut back once DORA began to apply. Amending guidelines published on 11 February 2025, applicable from 20 May 2025, limit them to managing the relationship with payment service users in the provision of payment services, and to entities that are also within DORA's scope. For buying and running third-party technology, the operative EU requirements for banks now sit in DORA rather than here. The amending reference EBA/GL/2025/02 was taken from EBA document titles rather than the EBA page text, which does not print it.
instruments.version: As amended by EBA/GL/2025/02 of 11 February 2025

instruments.name: Guidelines on outsourcing arrangements (EBA/GL/2019/02)
instruments.summary: The 2019 guidelines set expectations for banks, investment firms and payment and e-money institutions on outsourcing governance: identifying critical or important functions, due diligence and risk assessment, contract terms including access and audit rights, a register, monitoring and exit plans. On 18 September 2026 the EBA published final Guidelines on the sound management of third-party risk regarding non-ICT services (EBA/GL/2026/09), which will repeal the 2019 guidelines once applicable; the EBA lists them as awaiting translation and not yet applicable, and the application and repeal dates in the final report are still blank placeholders, with a two-year transition to follow. The replacement covers non-ICT services only and leaves third-party ICT services to DORA, so the 2019 text remains the applicable EBA guidance on the verification date but is on notice of repeal. The 30 September 2019 application date comes from EBA search excerpts and was not read directly from the 2019 document in this session.
instruments.version: EBA/GL/2019/02 of 25 February 2019; replacement EBA/GL/2026/09 is final but not yet applicable

instruments.issuer: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
instruments.name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data (General Data Protection Regulation)
instruments.summary: The GDPR governs how a bank and its suppliers handle personal data: a bank acting as controller needs a lawful basis, must use only processors that give sufficient guarantees under a written contract, must control sub-processing and transfers outside the EU, and must secure the data and report breaches. It entered into force on 24 May 2016 and has applied since 25 May 2018. EUR-Lex showed it as in force with corrigenda only and listed two Commission proposals to amend it (COM(2025) 501 and COM(2025) 837) that had not been adopted on the verification date.
instruments.version: OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, with corrigenda; no amending acts adopted (amendments proposed)

instruments.issuer: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
instruments.name: Directive (EU) 2022/2555 on measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union (NIS 2 Directive)
instruments.summary: NIS2 requires member states to impose cybersecurity risk management measures, including supply chain security, and incident reporting on essential and important entities across listed sectors, which include finance and many of the digital and ICT service providers banks buy from. It entered into force on 16 January 2023, had to be transposed by 17 October 2024, and national measures apply from 18 October 2024; because it is a directive, the binding detail sits in each member state's law. EUR-Lex showed it as in force with corrigenda only, plus two pending Commission proposals to amend it (COM(2025) 837 and COM(2026) 13), which had not been adopted on the verification date. How NIS2 interacts with DORA for banks was not stated on the pages checked.
instruments.version: OJ L 333, 27.12.2022; no amending acts adopted (amendments proposed)

instruments.name: ISO 22301:2019, Security and resilience - Business continuity management systems - Requirements
instruments.summary: The international requirements standard for a business continuity management system. It is relevant to a bank's operational resilience review of a vendor, as evidence that the vendor plans for, tests and recovers from disruption. ISO lists the second edition, published in October 2019 (month only), as current with one amendment (Amd 1:2024). Version caveat: the standard is at stage 90.92 (to be revised) and ISO shows a committee draft, ISO/CD 22301, under development to replace it.

instruments.name: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection - Information security management systems - Requirements
instruments.summary: The international requirements standard for an information security management system, against which organisations are certified by accredited bodies. Certification is one of the most common pieces of independent evidence a bank receives from a technology vendor, so the edition and the scope of the certificate both matter. ISO lists the third edition, published in October 2022 (month only, so no exact date is recorded), as current at stage 60.60, with one amendment on climate action changes (Amd 1:2024); the 2013 edition is withdrawn and no new edition is shown as under development.

instruments.name: ISO/IEC 27701:2025, Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection - Privacy information management systems - Requirements and guidance
instruments.summary: The international standard for a privacy information management system, covering how an organisation governs the personal data it handles. It helps a bank judge whether a vendor that handles customer data runs a structured, auditable privacy programme. Version caveat: ISO lists a second edition published in October 2025 (month only) as current and the 2019 edition as withdrawn, so vendor certificates that still cite ISO/IEC 27701:2019 refer to the earlier edition.

instruments.name: ISO/IEC 42001:2023, Information technology - Artificial intelligence - Management system
instruments.summary: The international requirements standard for an AI management system, setting out how an organisation should establish, run and improve its governance of AI. For a bank it is the main certifiable signal that an AI vendor has formal governance over its AI systems and their risks. ISO lists the first edition, published in December 2023 (month only), as current at stage 60.60, with no amendments and no revision shown as of 2026-11-20.

instruments.name: MITRE ATLAS
instruments.summary: A public knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques, mitigations and case studies for attacks on, and misuse of, AI systems. It gives a bank a concrete list of AI attack techniques against which to question an AI or AI-security vendor. ATLAS is now updated most months: the current data version is 2026.10 (October 2026 update on the ATLAS site; release dated 28 October 2026 in MITRE's data repository), covering 16 tactics, 129 techniques and 92 sub-techniques, so any vendor mapping should state the data version it used.

instruments.name: MITRE ATT&CK
instruments.summary: A public knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques, used as a common reference for describing what security tools detect and prevent. A bank can use it to test a security vendor's coverage claims technique by technique rather than accepting broad statements. MITRE lists v20 as current since 13 October 2026, with data releases 20.0 and 20.1, following v19 (April 2026) and v18 (October 2025); new major versions have been arriving about every six months, so vendor mappings should state the version used.

instruments.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
instruments.name: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
instruments.summary: A voluntary framework for identifying, measuring and managing risks from AI systems, released on 26 January 2023, with a Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) added on 26 July 2024. It gives a bank a structured way to ask how an AI vendor governs, tests and monitors its models. Version caveat: NIST's page states that AI RMF 1.0 is being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan, but as of 2026-11-20 it names no successor version or date, so 1.0 remains the current text; a critical-infrastructure profile is at concept-note stage (April 2026).

instruments.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
instruments.name: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0
instruments.summary: A voluntary framework that organises cybersecurity risk management outcomes into functions, categories and subcategories; version 2.0 (NIST CSWP 29) was published as final on 26 February 2024 and replaced version 1.1 of April 2018. Banks and their supervisors commonly use it as a shared vocabulary for comparing a vendor's security programme, and sector profiles such as the CRI Profile are built on it. As verified on 2026-11-20, NIST's pages show no CSF 2.1 or later revision, only new CSF 2.0 community profiles, quick-start guides and related drafts.

instruments.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
instruments.name: FIPS 140-3, Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules, with the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP)
instruments.summary: The US federal standard for cryptographic modules, defining four rising security levels; modules are tested by accredited laboratories and validated under the Cryptographic Module Validation Program run by NIST with the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security. For a bank it is one of the few vendor security claims that can be checked in a public registry: each certificate names the exact module and version, its overall level, its status and a sunset date, so 'FIPS validated' can be told apart from 'FIPS compliant' or a submission still in review. FIPS 140-3 superseded FIPS 140-2 and took effect on 22 September 2019; new validations sit on the active list for five years, or two years for interim validations. NIST's schedule moved all remaining FIPS 140-2 certificates to the historical list on 22 September 2026, where they are supported for existing systems only, so a vendor citing only a FIPS 140-2 certificate no longer holds an active validation.

instruments.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
instruments.name: FIPS 203, Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard
instruments.summary: The NIST standard for ML-KEM, a quantum-resistant method for establishing shared encryption keys, published as final on 13 August 2024. For a bank it is the reference point for judging whether a vendor's key exchange has a credible migration path away from algorithms that a quantum computer could break. NIST added a note in November 2025 that an identified issue will be corrected in a future update, so an errata revision should be expected. Further post-quantum standards are pending: NIST states FIPS 206 (FN-DSA, based on Falcon) is still in development and it does not appear in the FIPS list, and HQC was selected in March 2025 as a backup key-encapsulation algorithm with no draft standard listed as of 2026-11-20.

instruments.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
instruments.name: FIPS 204, Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard
instruments.summary: The NIST standard for ML-DSA, a quantum-resistant digital signature scheme, published as final on 13 August 2024. It matters to a bank when assessing how a vendor will protect code signing, certificates and transaction integrity against future quantum attack. A NIST note dated July 2026 lists several minor issues to be corrected in a future update, so an errata revision should be expected. Further post-quantum standards are pending: NIST states FIPS 206 (FN-DSA, based on Falcon) is still in development and it does not appear in the FIPS list, and HQC was selected in March 2025 as a backup key-encapsulation algorithm with no draft standard listed as of 2026-11-20.

instruments.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
instruments.name: FIPS 205, Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard
instruments.summary: The NIST standard for SLH-DSA, a quantum-resistant signature scheme that relies on hash functions rather than lattices, published as final on 13 August 2024. It gives a bank a second, mathematically different signature option to look for when judging a vendor's cryptographic agility. NIST's page shows no update or errata note for it as of 2026-11-20. Further post-quantum standards are pending: NIST states FIPS 206 (FN-DSA, based on Falcon) is still in development and it does not appear in the FIPS list, and HQC was selected in March 2025 as a backup key-encapsulation algorithm with no draft standard listed as of 2026-11-20.

instruments.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
instruments.name: NIST Risk Management Framework (SP 800-37)
instruments.summary: A seven-step process for managing security and privacy risk across a system's life: prepare, categorize, select, implement, assess, authorize and monitor. It tells an organisation how to choose, apply and keep checking the controls catalogued in NIST SP 800-53. A bank can use it to place a product in the step of its own risk process that the product helps with. The seven steps were read from NIST's project page on 2026-11-22; the publication's own date and its task-level identifiers were not read.

instruments.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
instruments.name: NIST SP 800-53, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations
instruments.summary: A catalogue of security and privacy controls, originally for US federal systems and widely used by vendors as a control baseline. A bank can use it to check the depth of a vendor's control set and to map vendor evidence to specific controls. Revision 5 dates from September 2020 (with updates to 10 December 2020); the current catalogue is the minor Release 5.2.0 issued on 27 August 2025, which added three controls or enhancements and revised others. The NIST publication page names no later release and no Revision 6; the interactive release catalogue could not be read directly in this check.

instruments.name: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025
instruments.summary: A community-maintained list of the ten most significant security risks in applications built on large language models, with mitigations. It is a practical checklist for a bank asking how an AI vendor handles LLM-specific risks, though it is awareness guidance rather than a certifiable standard. The current edition is the 2025 list, published by the OWASP GenAI Security Project on 17 November 2024, which followed the 2023-24 list (v1.1); no 2026 edition was released or announced on the project site as of 2026-11-20.

instruments.name: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS)
instruments.summary: The payment card industry's security standard for protecting payment account data. A bank should expect a vendor in the card payment flow to be validated against it and should check which version the validation used. The current version in the PCI SSC document library is v4.0.1, a limited revision announced on 11 June 2024; PCI SSC stated that v4.0 would be retired on 31 December 2024 and that the future-dated requirements would take effect on 31 March 2025. No later version was shown as of 2026-11-20.

instruments.name: SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2) examination against the Trust Services Criteria
instruments.summary: An independent CPA examination and report on a service organisation's controls for security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy, measured against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria. A SOC 2 report is often the main third-party assurance a bank obtains from a technology vendor, so its period, scope and exceptions need reading. The criteria published by the AICPA are the 2017 Trust Services Criteria with points of focus revised in 2022; the AICPA pages checked do not label an edition as current in so many words. Version caveat: on 28 October 2026 the AICPA announced exposure drafts of proposed 2027 Trust Services Criteria and Description Criteria, including AI-related points of focus, with comments due 15 January 2027 and, if approved, application to engagements beginning on or after 31 December 2027.
instruments.version: 2017 Trust Services Criteria (With Revised Points of Focus - 2022)

instruments.issuer: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority (designation by HM Treasury)
instruments.name: Critical third parties to the UK financial sector: rules (PRA PS16/24 / FCA PS24/16) and supervisory statement SS6/24
instruments.summary: This regime places resilience, incident-reporting and testing duties directly on technology and other suppliers that HM Treasury designates as critical to the UK financial sector, overseen jointly by the Bank of England, PRA and FCA. The rules were published on 12 November 2024 and took effect on 1 January 2025, but bind a provider only from the date its designation comes into force. The first designations took effect on 13 July 2026 under the Critical Third Parties (Designation) Regulations 2026: Amazon Web Services EMEA SARL, Google Cloud EMEA Limited, Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited and Oracle Corporation UK Limited. The duties fall on the designated provider, and the regulators state that designation does not reduce a bank's own accountability for its outsourcing and operational resilience.
instruments.version: Rules and SS6/24 published 12 November 2024; first designations made by S.I. 2026/777

instruments.name: FCA Handbook SYSC 8 (Outsourcing), with related outsourcing provisions in SYSC 13 and guidance FG16/5
instruments.summary: The FCA's outsourcing requirements sit mainly in SYSC 8 of its Handbook (SYSC 8.1 covers general outsourcing requirements, including for critical or important operational functions), with further provisions in SYSC 13 and guidance FG16/5 on cloud and other third-party IT services for firms not covered by the EBA outsourcing guidelines. A firm stays responsible for functions it hands to a supplier, must manage the added operational risk, and must tell the FCA about material outsourcing. The Handbook showed SYSC 8.1 as last updated on 23 October 2025 with a future version dated 18 March 2027, the day the FCA's new operational incident and third-party reporting rules (PS26/2, published 18 March 2026) start to apply; those rules add notification of material third-party arrangements and an annual register. The original commencement date of SYSC 8 was not shown on the FCA pages checked, so effectiveDate is left empty.
instruments.version: SYSC 8.1 as last updated 23 October 2025; a future version is scheduled for 18 March 2027

instruments.issuer: Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority
instruments.name: Operational resilience: Impact tolerances for important business services (PRA SS1/21) and FCA operational resilience rules (PS21/3, SYSC 15A)
instruments.summary: Firms must identify their important business services, set an impact tolerance for disruption to each, map the people, processes, technology and suppliers that deliver them, and test that they can stay within tolerance in severe but plausible scenarios, which makes the resilience of third-party technology a direct concern. The PRA statement and the FCA rules in SYSC 15A both took effect on 31 March 2022, and the FCA states the transition period for being able to remain within tolerances ended on 31 March 2025. The PRA page lists the March 2022 version of SS1/21 as current with no later revision. Separate operational incident and third-party reporting rules from both regulators (PRA PS7/26 with new SS1/26, FCA PS26/2) were published on 18 March 2026 and apply from 18 March 2027.
instruments.version: PRA SS1/21 version published 11 March 2022 (effective 31 March 2022); FCA rules per PS21/3

instruments.name: SS1/23 - Model risk management principles for banks
instruments.summary: Sets out the PRA's principles for managing model risk across a bank: identifying and tiering models, governance, development and use, independent validation, and mitigants, and the PRA's page says this extends to risks from artificial intelligence and machine learning used in modelling. For bought-in or vendor-supplied models this means the bank needs enough information and control to apply the same standards. SS1/23 was published on 17 May 2023 and took effect on 17 May 2024; the current version dates from 23 April 2026, when a low-impact amendment clarified that the expectations are not conditions for internal model approval and gave newly permissioned internal-model firms 12 months to meet them. No consultation on replacing SS1/23 was shown on the PRA page.
instruments.version: Version published and effective 23 April 2026 (following LIAF01/26)

instruments.name: SS2/21 - Outsourcing and third party risk management
instruments.summary: Sets the PRA's expectations for how banks, building societies, PRA-designated investment firms and insurers govern outsourcing and other third-party arrangements across their life cycle, including cloud and other technology services. SS2/21 was first published on 29 March 2021 and took effect on 31 March 2022; the version in force on the verification date is the one published on 15 November 2024. An updated version issued with PS7/26 on 18 March 2026 becomes effective on 18 March 2027: it revises the chapter on material third-party arrangements to fit new PRA rules requiring firms to notify the PRA before entering or significantly changing such arrangements and to file an annual register of them. The PRA's page lists no replacement for SS2/21 itself.
instruments.version: Current version published 15 November 2024, effective 31 December 2024; updated version published 18 March 2026 takes effect 18 March 2027

instruments.name: FedRAMP (Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program) Certification
instruments.summary: The US federal government's programme for assessing the security of cloud services used by agencies, with results published in the public FedRAMP Marketplace. It matters to a bank as independent, registry-checkable evidence about a vendor's cloud offering, but a listing covers only the named offering (often a separate government environment) and the status shown, not the vendor's commercial service. The programme was restructured in 2026: the Consolidated Rules for 2026 launched on 24 June 2026 (the date recorded here) and become mandatory on 1 January 2027; 'FedRAMP Certified' is now the programme's term for what was called authorised, and offerings carry a type (the legacy Rev5 or the newer 20x, which is based on measured outcomes), a path (agency or programme) and a class from A to D, with the Marketplace equating Class B to Low and LI-SaaS, Class C to Moderate and Class D to High. FedRAMP Ready became a legacy status after 28 July 2026, and FedRAMP has said it will stop accepting applications for new Rev5 certifications after 11 June 2027.
instruments.version: Consolidated Rules for 2026; certification types Rev5 and 20x, Classes A to D

instruments.name: FFIEC Information Technology Examination Handbook
instruments.summary: A set of examiner booklets, not a single dated document, describing what examiners look for in a bank's IT governance, information security, architecture and operations, development and acquisition of systems, business continuity, audit, payment systems and outsourcing of technology services, plus how the agencies supervise technology service providers directly. For a bank buying technology, the Outsourcing Technology Services and the Development, Acquisition, and Maintenance booklets are the most relevant: they cover provider selection, due diligence, contract terms, ongoing monitoring and supply-chain considerations. The handbook has no single effective date; the most recent booklet revision is Development, Acquisition, and Maintenance (29 August 2024, replacing the 2004 Development and Acquisition booklet), and the latest handbook-wide change, on 27 February 2026, removed references to reputational risk without adding requirements.

instruments.issuer: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
instruments.name: Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards (implementing Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act section 501(b))
instruments.summary: Requires a bank to run a written, board-approved information security program that protects customer information, based on a risk assessment, and to oversee its service providers: due diligence in selecting them, contract terms obliging them to apply appropriate safeguards, and monitoring (such as reviewing audits and test results) where the bank's risk assessment calls for it. An attached supplement covers response programs for unauthorized access to customer information, including provider notification to the bank. Banks had to implement the program by 1 July 2001; the text has been amended several times since, most recently by the OCC and FDIC reputation-risk rule (published 10 April 2026, effective 9 June 2026), which made a small wording change to the incident-response supplement and left the service-provider provisions unchanged. The OCC version was read on the eCFR, current to 18 November 2026; the Board and FDIC parallel texts were not read line by line.
instruments.version: 12 CFR Part 30 Appendix B (OCC), with parallel text at Part 208 Appendix D-2 (Board) and Part 364 Appendix B (FDIC); OCC and FDIC text as amended at 91 FR 18293, 10 April 2026

instruments.issuer: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
instruments.name: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management
instruments.summary: Asks a bank to manage each third-party relationship, technology and AI suppliers included, across its whole life cycle (planning, due diligence and selection, contracting, ongoing monitoring and termination), with the depth of oversight scaled to the risk and to how critical the supported activity is; the bank stays responsible for the outsourced activity. Issued 6 June 2023, it replaced each agency's earlier general third-party guidance (for the OCC, Bulletins 2013-29 and 2020-10; for the Federal Reserve, SR 13-19). Status caveat: on 11 September 2026 the OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC and NCUA proposed replacement guidance (91 FR 58536) that would rescind this guidance and its supplements, drop the emphasis on critical activities in favour of risk-based tailoring, and be expressly non-enforceable; the comment period was extended to 16 December 2026 and nothing is final, so the 2023 guidance is still the current text as of the verification date.

instruments.issuer: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
instruments.name: Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management
instruments.summary: This is the current US model risk guidance: issued 17 April 2026, it superseded the 2011 guidance (SR 11-7 / OCC Bulletin 2011-12) and the 2021 interagency statement on BSA/AML models (SR 21-8 / OCC Bulletin 2021-19), and the OCC also rescinded its Model Risk Management handbook booklet and Bulletin 1997-24. It sets out risk-based, principles-level practices for developing, validating, governing and using models, including considerations for validating vendor and other third-party products, is described as most relevant to banks above 30 billion dollars in assets, and states that it does not create enforceable standards. Important scope caveat for AI purchases: per the OCC bulletin, generative and agentic AI models are excluded, and the agencies say they plan a separate request for information on banks' use of AI. Neither issuer page states an effective date; the issue date is recorded.

instruments.issuer: New York State Department of Financial Services
instruments.name: 23 NYCRR Part 500: Cybersecurity Requirements for Financial Services Companies
instruments.summary: Binding cybersecurity rules for entities licensed by the New York DFS: a risk-based cybersecurity program and policies, a CISO reporting to the senior governing body, access controls, encryption, penetration testing and vulnerability management, incident response and continuity planning, notification of cybersecurity events to DFS, annual certification, and written policies governing the security of third-party service providers. The regulation dates from 1 March 2017; the Second Amendment took effect on 1 November 2023 with staged dates, the last of which (multi-factor authentication for all individuals accessing information systems and a documented asset inventory) applied from 1 November 2025, so the amended text now applies in full. DFS's rulemaking page showed no proposed or emergency amendment to Part 500 on the verification date; DFS has instead issued non-binding industry letters, including ones in 2026 on frontier AI cyber risk and on risk assessments.
instruments.version: As amended by the Second Amendment (adopted and effective 1 November 2023; phased requirements fully applicable from 1 November 2025)

regulatoryActions.value: The Associated Press reported on 2026-09-25 that the US Defense Secretary designated Anthropic a supply chain risk in February 2026, and that a federal appeals court in Washington ruled 2-1 that the Pentagon may keep the designation and bar Anthropic products from Defense Department work, including by contractors. Al Jazeera reported on 2026-08-28 that a federal district judge in California had ruled the designation unlawful, finding it followed Anthropic's public refusal to allow use of its models for domestic surveillance or autonomous weapons. AP reported that Anthropic said it disagreed with the appeals ruling and was considering further review, and that the ruling does not bar its products across the federal government. Il Sole 24 Ore reported on 2026-06-13 that Anthropic disabled its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models for all customers three days after their launch, after receiving a US government directive on 2026-06-12, issued under export-control rules on national-security grounds, that required it to suspend access for foreign nationals; the report states that Anthropic said the action did not meet the standard of a transparent and fair process. By its account attackers obtained a privileged token from Trivy's GitHub Actions environment in late February 2026; an incident was disclosed on 1 March but credential rotation was incomplete; on 2026-03-19 a malicious Trivy v0.69.4 release was published and version tags of the trivy-action and setup-trivy GitHub Actions were redirected to malicious code for up to about 12 hours; on 2026-03-22 malicious Docker Hub images appeared and internal repositories were published. regulatoryActions.value: Italy's Garante announced on 2025-01-30 that it had ordered DeepSeek's two operating companies to limit processing of Italian users' data and opened an investigation, stating that the companies' reply was wholly insufficient. The US Department of Homeland Security published on 2026-10-20 an order dated 2026-07-24 excluding DeepSeek products from federal civilian agency procurement and systems, stating that its servers are in China and that Chinese law gives government bodies broad access to company infrastructure. CISA, the NSA and the FBI published an advisory on 2026-09-08 alleging that DeepSeek and five other China-based companies distilled US companies' models in breach of terms of use. NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation published an evaluation on 2025-09-30 reporting that DeepSeek models were more susceptible to agent hijacking and jailbreaking than US reference models. The Berlin data protection commissioner published a notice to Apple and Google describing the DeepSeek app as illegal content in June 2025. Global News and The Canadian Press reported on 2025-02-07 that the app was restricted on Canadian government mobile devices managed by Shared Services Canada. A Reuters factbox of 2026-01-07 also lists public-sector bans in the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, Australia and Taiwan and a download suspension in South Korea that was later lifted; those were not verified against the issuing bodies in this session. No measure by a UK authority was found.

securityIncidents.value: Disclosed by F5 in a Form 8-K filed 2025-10-15: a nation-state threat actor had long-term access to systems including the BIG-IP product development environment and an engineering knowledge platform, discovered on 2025-08-09, and exfiltrated files including portions of BIG-IP source code and information on undisclosed vulnerabilities. F5 stated it found no evidence of software supply-chain modification, and that some files contained configuration or implementation information for a small percentage of customers. CyberScoop reported the disclosure the same day. F5's FY2026 10-K reported $28.0 million of related expenses and stated the incident had not had a material impact on operations or financial condition to date.

securityIncidents.value: Fireworks AI disclosed in security bulletins dated 2026-10-10, 2026-11-09 and 2026-11-17 two incidents. In the first, running from 2026-08-03 to 2026-10-07 and detected on 2026-10-06, an unauthorised party used stolen Fireworks credentials and a service vulnerability and obtained API keys and tokens stored as secrets for evaluation jobs. In the second, from 2026-10-23 to 2026-10-30, an attacker reached development machines through a compromised third-party cloud provider and then part of production. The company stated that account and billing information for all accounts created before 2026-10-30 was accessed and that secrets, datasets and models were accessed for a small number of customers; it reported no detected impact on inference traffic, which is not retained by default. It described both incidents as contained and remediated on 2026-11-17, with forensic work on the second continuing. The Register and BleepingComputer reported the disclosures on 2026-11-10.

litigation.value: Alphabet disclosed in its 2025 Form 10-K and its Form 10-Q for the third quarter of 2026: a final judgment in December 2025 in the US Department of Justice search case, imposing distribution restrictions and data-sharing and syndication duties, under appeal by both sides; a September 2026 remedies decision in the US advertising technology case that denied divestiture and ordered behavioural remedies; court approval in August 2026 of the Google Play settlement with state attorneys general and continued compliance with the Epic Games remedies; a Swedish court award of about US$2.1 billion to PriceRunner in July 2026, under appeal; and a US$1.4 billion settlement of certain privacy matters finalised in October 2025. The filings also note patent, copyright and AI-related claims in general terms.

regulatoryActions.value: Alphabet disclosed in its 2025 Form 10-K and its Form 10-Q for the third quarter of 2026: a European Commission decision in September 2025 fining Google EUR 3.0 billion over advertising technology, which Google appealed; a Japan Fair Trade Commission cease-and-desist order in April 2025 over Android agreements; a settlement with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission approved in December 2025; the EUR 4.1 billion Android fine becoming final in July 2026, with a US$5.2 billion payment; and Digital Markets Act non-compliance decisions in July 2026 with fines of EUR 430 million (Google Play) and EUR 460 million (Search), appealed in October 2026. Computerworld and the Irish Examiner reported on 2025-12-09 that the European Commission opened an antitrust investigation into Google's use of publisher content and YouTube videos for its AI models. None of these is attributed to the Gemini API, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform or Gemini Enterprise as enterprise services.

securityIncidents.value: Reported by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer on 2025-08-06: Google disclosed that one of its corporate Salesforce instances was accessed in June 2025 by a group it tracks as UNC6040, and that contact details and related notes for small and medium businesses were taken during a short window before access was cut off. Alphabet stated in its 2025 Form 10-K that it experiences cyber attacks and attempts at unauthorised access on a regular basis. Google also published reports on a Google Cloud outage on 12 June 2025 and a Gemini API disruption on 27 February 2026, recorded under each product's incident history.

securityIncidents.value: Reported by The Register on 2026-11-16 and by Cyber Daily on 2026-11-17: Infoblox said it was investigating unauthorised access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor. The Register, citing sources and an email from the chief executive, reported that the intruders used the vendor's access to Infoblox's SharePoint and that the data included personal and payroll details of employees and their dependants and saved configuration snapshots of some customers' NIOS deployments. A company spokesperson told both outlets there was no indication that Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved. Infoblox did not say how many customers or employees were affected.

leadershipIssues.value: The 10-K shows that Clayton Magouyrk and Michael Sicilia have both held the title of Chief Executive Officer since September 2025, with Lawrence J. Ellison remaining executive chair and chief technology officer. The securities class action filed in February 2026 names senior executives as defendants. No other leadership matter was found in the filings read.

litigation.note: Court dockets were not searched in this session.
litigation.value: According to Oracle's Form 10-K for fiscal 2026 and Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 2026-08-31: (1) a putative securities class action was filed on 2026-02-03 in the US District Court for the District of Delaware alleging false and misleading statements about Oracle's cloud infrastructure business; an amended complaint was filed on 2026-07-14 and names the company, its chief technology officer, one of its chief executive officers, two other executives and a director. (2) A Dutch privacy class action brought in 2020 by The Privacy Collective over Oracle's Data Management Platform, claiming damages under the GDPR, continues; on 2026-07-17 the Dutch Supreme Court remanded the case to the Court of Appeal. Oracle states that it has meritorious defences to both and does not expect a material impact.

regulatoryActions.note: Not searched: SEC administrative proceedings list, state attorneys general, banking supervisors, data-protection authorities and non-US regulators.
regulatoryActions.value: According to the SEC's press release of 2022-09-27, Oracle agreed to pay more than US$23 million to settle charges that it violated the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act through subsidiaries in Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and India between 2016 and 2019; the SEC noted it had previously sanctioned Oracle in 2012 over Oracle India. The SEC litigation release list shows release LR-22450 (2012-08-16) naming Oracle Corporation. The FTC cases library lists one administrative matter, 'Oracle Corporation, In the Matter of' (file 132 3115), last updated 2016-03-29. No later enforcement action naming Oracle was found in those two registers when searched on 2026-11-21.

securityIncidents.note: Neither incident concerns Oracle AI Database or the current-generation OCI services as described by Oracle. Medium confidence because Oracle's account and the researchers' accounts of the 2025 cloud incident differ.
securityIncidents.value: Reported by BleepingComputer on 2025-04-03 and Security Affairs on 2025-04-10: Oracle told some customers that an attacker had taken credentials from older systems, described by Oracle as two obsolete servers that were never part of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, while a threat actor offered about 6 million records for sale; Oracle said no Oracle Cloud Infrastructure systems or customer data were affected, which researchers quoted in those reports disputed. Separately, Oracle published Security Alert CVE-2025-61882 on 2025-10-04 for a remotely exploitable flaw in Oracle E-Business Suite, and The Record reported on 2025-10-03 that Oracle confirmed customers had received extortion emails from the Clop group. Oracle's 10-K states that malicious attacks have led to the compromise of personal or confidential information of Oracle or its customers.

lastRound.reason: Listed company; no private rounds. Debt and preferred stock issues are described in runwaySignals.

layoffs.value: According to Oracle's Form 10-K for fiscal 2026, management approved a Fiscal 2026 Oracle Restructuring Plan with total estimated costs of up to US$2.1 billion, of which US$1.8 billion was recorded in fiscal 2026 (US$299 million of restructuring expense in fiscal 2025). The filing says the expenses are employee severance costs and that adopting AI across its operations has resulted, and may continue to result, in workforce reductions. The number of positions affected is not stated.

publicFinancials.value: Fiscal 2026 (year ended 2026-05-31): revenue US$67,357M, up 17% from US$57,399M; operating income US$20,606M; net income US$17,087M, against US$12,443M in fiscal 2025. Cloud revenue was US$33,989M (51% of the total). First quarter of fiscal 2027 (ended 2026-08-31): revenue US$19,345M and net income US$4,760M.

runwaySignals.value: Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities were US$31.9 billion at 2026-05-31 and about US$37.1 billion at 2026-08-31. Fiscal 2026 capital expenditure was US$55.7 billion, funded in part by US$43.0 billion of senior notes and US$5.0 billion of mandatory convertible preferred stock issued in the year. Notes payable and other borrowings were about US$125 billion at 2026-08-31. Remaining performance obligations were US$638 billion at 2026-05-31 and US$664 billion at 2026-08-31, of which about 13% is expected to be recognised within twelve months. The 10-K says returns on its data-centre investment depend on key customers meeting their contractual obligations.

litigation.value: According to Pegasystems' Form 10-K for 2025 and Form 10-Q for the third quarter of 2026, the company is defendant in Appian Corp. v. Pegasystems Inc. & Youyong Zou in Fairfax County, Virginia. A jury found in May 2022 that it had misappropriated Appian trade secrets wilfully and maliciously, and judgment of US$2,060 million was entered in September 2022. The Court of Appeals of Virginia reversed and ordered a new trial in July 2024 and the Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed that on 2026-01-08. The retrial is set to begin on 2027-01-11. On 2026-10-16 the court allowed Appian to present a reasonable-royalty damages theory, under which it seeks US$284.6 million and US$1.36 billion; the company states that it denies misappropriation and cannot reasonably estimate possible damages. The 10-Q also reports that two sets of securities lawsuits brought by investors who opted out of a settled class action were settled on 2026-09-18 and dismissed with prejudice in October 2026, that a shareholder derivative case was settled with court approval on 2026-06-30, and that a US$16 million loss was accrued for litigation settlements. The company is plaintiff in a separate defamation case against Appian in the District of Massachusetts, in which Appian has counterclaimed.

products.description: Anthropic's agentic coding tool. It reads a codebase, edits files and runs commands from the terminal, VS Code and JetBrains extensions, a desktop app, the web and mobile apps, GitHub Actions and Slack. Organisations get it through Claude Team or Enterprise seats, through the Claude Console at API rates, or by pointing it at Claude models on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud or Microsoft Foundry. The ownership start date is the first day of May 2025, the month in which TechRadar says the product became generally available; the exact day was not found.

independentTests.result: Claude Code's best entries resolved 65.8% of tasks (with Opus 5.5, entered 2026-09-22, and with Fable 5.2, entered 2026-11-09), joint second behind GitHub Copilot at 71.2%. Entries with other models ranged down to 6.7%. The leaderboard had 54 rows when read on 2026-11-22; the page does not say who ran or verified each entry.

Claude Code resolved 60.4% of problems (plus or minus 1.03), ranked 7th, with 75.7% solved in at least one of five attempts and a cost of US$3.39 a problem, the highest of the four agent products listed. Task window 15 May to 1 July 2026 (111 problems from 65 repositories); 117 rows, led by a bare model at 64.5%. The SWE-rebench team says it runs all evaluations itself.

support.note: The platform parses, normalises and enriches feeds into the customer's data store and can pull alerts from security tools. Its documentation says it supplies no forwarding agent or streaming tool, and that raw log ingestion is supported for Snowflake but not for Splunk; the customer's own store holds the logs.
The vendor cites a library of more than 3,500 detections mapped to MITRE ATT&CK and updated weekly, correlated multi-stage scenarios, detection version control and automated tuning recommendations.
One search across connected SIEMs, data lakes and cloud storage in natural language or query languages, with results in one view, plus built-in case management.
Blueprints chain agents into workflows with approval steps and can trigger containment through connected tools such as an endpoint product or identity provider, or hand a case to an existing SOAR.

The platform does not retain logs itself. The vendor says it can index and search long-retention archives left in the customer's own cloud storage. How long data is kept is decided by the customer's store, not the product.

Data stays in tables in the customer's own Snowflake or Databricks account or in its own cloud storage, and can be normalised to OCSF, Splunk's CIM or a custom schema. The vendor says detections and workflows move with the customer.
A triage agent gives each alert a verdict with a summary and timeline, and investigation workflows gather evidence before an analyst opens the case. Performance figures are the vendor's own.

support.note: The Palo Alto Networks release, blog and datasheet describe passive discovery of publicly exposed assets, cloud resources and exposed secrets as the first step of the external assessment, and the TENEX.ai release says the agents mapped the external perimeter of the institution tested into a knowledge graph. All four are the vendor's releases or its reselling partner's material; how assets unknown to the customer are attributed to it is not described.

The product's main function. Agents attempt exploitation and, where access is gained, simulate post-exploitation behaviour; the Unit 42 material says each attack chain is logged as evidence of exploitable risk and cites more than 50,000 templates. The vendor says the attacks are run safely against production networks. What the proof consists of (for example captured output or screenshots) is not described, and no independent test of the product was found.

The vendor says the agents chain individually low-severity weaknesses into validated kill chains, with an example running from unauthenticated remote code execution at the perimeter through lateral movement to cloud compromise, and that each path is shown with its blast radius. It reported 38 validated attack paths in an August 2026 exercise against an unnamed institution. Press coverage repeats the vendor's account.

The CrowdStrike release says the agents run against an enterprise's internal network, including infrastructure, identity and endpoints, and the TENEX.ai release lists the internal network in the scope of the August 2026 exercise. A BankInfoSecurity interview with a co-founder says the agents evaluate identity risks as they emerge. No source names directory services or describes which identity attacks are attempted, and how the agents are placed inside the network is not described.

Web applications are named as one of the areas attacked, in the TENEX.ai release, in BankInfoSecurity's launch report and in an investor's note. None describes the testing, such as authenticated testing or business-logic flaws, and API testing is not mentioned in any source read. In the TENEX.ai release, API categories appear only in how the defending partner classified the findings.

Safeguards and human oversight are claimed in general terms: every agent action passes through a control layer supervised by a safety model trained on feedback from human experts, SiliconANGLE reports that agents run in a sandbox meant to block harmful activity, and human red-team staff review findings and validate complex chains. How a customer sets and enforces what is in scope, what actions are barred on production systems and how a campaign is stopped are not described.

The product gives prioritised remediation guidance: BankInfoSecurity reports that it ranks fixes by whether they would break whole attack chains, and the vendor's site summary says guidance is ranked by business impact. Re-running an attack to confirm a fix is not described in any vendor, partner or press source read; the vendor describes testing as continuous, which is not the same thing. In the CrowdStrike arrangement remediation is done by CrowdStrike and its partners.

Customers receive the proven paths, their potential impact and prioritised remediation guidance. The vendor has no separate name for the platform; its assessment offering is called Armadin Red, and the technology is also sold as an external assessment through Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 and through CrowdStrike. Public material is press releases, partner pages and press reports; no technical documentation could be read.

Central key and policy management across integrated AWS services and the customer's applications, with multi-Region keys. The scope is AWS services and applications that call KMS; management of keys held in other clouds or on-premises systems is not described.

Import of the customer's own key material, a custom key store in the customer's CloudHSM cluster, and an external key store in which keys stay in a key manager outside AWS. External key stores support symmetric encryption keys only and exclude import, automatic rotation and multi-Region keys.

Protection of data in use comes from AWS Nitro Enclaves, an Amazon EC2 feature: KMS verifies an enclave's signed attestation document so that only that enclave can use a key. It is not a function of KMS or CloudHSM alone.

products.description: AWS's key services. AWS Key Management Service (KMS), introduced on 12 November 2014, creates and controls the keys that AWS services and applications use to encrypt and sign data, holding them in hardware security modules validated to FIPS 140-3 Security Level 3. Keys can be generated by KMS, imported, kept in a customer-owned AWS CloudHSM cluster, or held outside AWS in the customer's own key manager through an external key store. AWS CloudHSM provides single-tenant HSMs in the customer's VPC.

exitAndSubstitutability.value: Keys generated in KMS HSMs cannot be exported in plaintext, so data must be re-encrypted to leave. The external key store proxy API specification is published as open source and vendors including Thales, Entrust, Fortanix, Utimaco and HashiCorp are named as offering compatible key managers.

support.note: Quick Index and knowledge bases bring content from sources such as Amazon S3, SharePoint, OneDrive, Confluence, Google Drive and web crawlers into retrieval, and keep the index in sync.

For knowledge bases created with document-level access control lists, synchronised permissions are enforced on every retrieval, and no documents are returned if permissions cannot be evaluated. Quick Research delivers cited reports, and chat log records carry a list of cited resources.

Role-based access, custom permissions with a deny-by-default option for AI capabilities, per-connector permissions and AWS Organizations service control policies. Custom permissions require an Enterprise subscription.

support.note: S3 Vectors: up to 2 billion vectors per index and 10,000 indexes per bucket, with metadata filtering. OpenSearch Service: knn_vector fields of up to 16,000 dimensions with exact and approximate (HNSW) search.
S3 Vectors documentation describes full-text (BM25) and hybrid queries on a vector index, and describes OpenSearch Service as the option for advanced hybrid search, aggregations and faceted search.

OpenSearch Service fine-grained access control gives role-based security at index, document and field level. S3 Vectors access is controlled with IAM and service control policies down to an individual vector index, not to individual vectors.
The open-source OpenSearch software can be run by the customer, but that is then not the AWS service. S3 Vectors has no self-managed form.
OpenSearch is licensed under Apache 2.0 and began in 2021 as a fork of Elasticsearch and Kibana. S3 Vectors is a proprietary AWS service.
S3 Vectors supports SSE-KMS with customer managed keys at bucket or index level, fixed at creation. OpenSearch Service encrypts data at rest through AWS KMS, with symmetric customer keys supported.

products.description: AWS's two native vector stores, recorded together because AWS positions them as tiers of one design. Amazon S3 Vectors is vector storage and query built into S3 (vector buckets and indexes, up to 2 billion vectors per index), generally available since 2 December 2025 and aimed at large, less frequently queried data. products.description: Check Point's product for securing the AI applications and agents an organisation builds, part of its AI Defense Plane portfolio. It is the continuation of Lakera Guard, the runtime product of Lakera AI AG, a Swiss company Check Point acquired in October 2025. Its runtime layer, AI Guardrails (also sold separately, as SaaS or a self-hosted container), screens prompts, model outputs, tool calls and tool responses through the Guard API for prompt attacks, data leakage, harmful content and unsafe agent actions. Agent discovery and per-agent risk assessment were added in early access in June 2026. Lakera's testing product is sold separately as Check Point AI Red Teaming, and employee AI use is covered by a separate product, Workforce AI Security. Documentation remains at docs.lakera.ai.

products.description: Cloud-delivered endpoint security on the Falcon platform, using a single sensor on each endpoint managed from a web console. Modules include Falcon Prevent (next-generation antivirus), Falcon Insight XDR (detection and response) and Falcon Complete (managed detection and response), with Falcon Next-Gen SIEM for wider data. The vendor's site now markets the line as agentic endpoint security.

independentTests.result: CrowdStrike Falcon scored 95% protection accuracy, 100% legitimate accuracy and 98% total accuracy, the lowest protection accuracy of the seven products; it stopped 98 of 100 threats and was compromised twice, both in targeted attacks. It still received the AAA award.
CrowdStrike Falcon scored 100% for protection accuracy, legitimate accuracy and total accuracy, one of three of the six products with a full score, and received the AAA award.

In a single-product ransomware test, CrowdStrike Falcon scored 100% on detection (360/360), protection (2,596/2,596), legitimate (640/640) and total accuracy (3,596/3,596) with no false positives, and received the AAA award. SE Labs says single-product reports of this kind are paid for by the vendor.
independentTests.round: Advanced Security EDR (Protection), ransomware, tested September-October 2025

independentTests.result: CrowdStrike Falcon Enterprise blocked 98.5% of real-world test cases with 8 false alarms, and 99.7% in the malware protection test with none on common business software. Its performance impact score of 36.2 ranked 13th of 16, and it was listed among products with above-average false positives on non-business software. It received the Approved Business Product award.

CrowdStrike Falcon Enterprise was certified with 97.3% active response, 98.0% passive response and a combined 97.7%, at a modelled five-year cost of $1,245 per agent; six of the ten named products scored higher on the combined measure. CrowdStrike is not among the eleven vendors named in the 2026 round.

MITRE's results page shows CrowdStrike with 89 of 90 detection sub-steps graded Technique (the highest grade) and 1 graded None in the initial run across the Scattered Spider and Mustang Panda scenarios; with the configuration-change run switched on, all 90 are graded Technique. In the protection tests MITRE shows CrowdStrike as Protected in all five scored tests it has results for (credential theft, unmanaged to managed devices, initial access malware execution, malware execution and lateral movement, AWS compromise); the identity provider test was withdrawn for every participant, and the false-positive test is shown as 'Not reported'. MITRE publishes counts, not percentages, and does not rank participants.

support.note: Registered models and versions sit in a three-level namespace with owners, aliases, tags and lineage, visible from any workspace attached to the metastore; model, MCP and agent services are also governed objects. A register of AI use cases or business initiatives, as distinct from technical assets, was not described.
Governed tags with enforced allowed values can label models and model versions, and access policies can be driven by tags. No built-in risk classification or tier-driven control set is described.

Deployment jobs can gate a model version behind an approval task; the approver clicks Approve on the model version page, which is recorded as a Unity Catalog tag and in the activity log, and governed tag policies can restrict who approves. Deployment jobs are in Public Preview and the documentation calls the approval mechanism experimental.

A deployment job's evaluation task runs MLflow evaluation and its metrics appear on the model version page for approvers. The feature is in Public Preview; bias and robustness tests are not specifically described.

Generative AI evaluation with LLM judges and code-based scorers is provided by MLflow on the same platform and can run inside a deployment job; it is not a function of Unity Catalog itself, and results are stored with traces in MLflow experiments.

External model providers and MCP servers are registered and governed through Unity Gateway with permissions, rate limits, guardrail policies and usage and spend tracking. Supplier assessment, such as questionnaires or contract and due-diligence records, is not described.
The product overview and documentation describe access control, lineage, auditing and monitoring; maintained mappings or templates for named regulations are outside the product's stated scope.
Data profiling (formerly Lakehouse Monitoring) monitors inference tables to track model performance and drift against a baseline or between time windows, with alerts on changes.

Audit, lineage and usage data are queryable and the vendor describes a single view of governance, cost and AI usage. Generated documentation or report packs for auditors, boards or supervisors are not described.

support.note: Model, agent and bundle registries are built from items synced from Dataiku nodes, with Govern projects and business initiatives created in Govern, including projects at the idea stage. Registration of models built outside Dataiku was not confirmed.

Governing an item applies a qualification process, and scripted policies (Advanced licence) can apply rules by tags or AI type. Business initiatives and governed projects have a Matrix view whose axes the documentation read does not describe; a built-in risk classification was not confirmed.

Each governed item follows a templated workflow with a sign-off that collects reviewer feedback and a final approval, with delegation. A deployment policy can block or warn on deployment of unapproved model versions and bundles; the default is to deploy without checking.

The Model registry shows model status, performance and deployment metrics against each model version. The tests themselves run in other Dataiku nodes; recording of bias or robustness tests in Govern was not confirmed.

Agents, augmented LLMs and fine-tuned LLMs appear in an Agent registry and can be governed with the Advanced licence. LLM evaluation is a feature of the Dataiku platform; whether its results are shown in Govern was not confirmed.
The vendor says agents can be tracked inside and outside Dataiku, and custom items can be created in Govern. Supplier assessment for bought-in models or AI services is not described.

Dataiku offers an EU AI Act Readiness solution with a ready-made governance workflow and blueprints, and its Knowledge Base lists an ISO 42001 Readiness solution. How often the content is maintained was not stated.
The Model registry lets reviewers track input drift alongside performance and deployment metrics; the monitoring runs in the Dataiku platform and is surfaced in Govern.

Matrix and Kanban views, a Timeline of item events and custom pages are documented, and the vendor describes automated documentation. Generated report packs for auditors, boards or supervisors were not confirmed.

products.description: Governance node of the Dataiku platform. support.note: Physical, virtual and cloud packet sensors receive a copy of traffic and the system discovers and classifies devices from it; the vendor says no agents or inline appliances are needed.

Machine-learning models baseline individual devices and groups of similar devices and raise a detection when activity deviates. The models run in the vendor's cloud service; disconnected systems use uploaded detector packs.

Rule-based detections for known exploit attempts and attack tools, built-in and imported (STIX, TAXII) threat collections, and signature detections from a curated ruleset. The signature detections need the separately licensed IDS module and an IDS sensor.

Decrypts TLS, using forwarded session keys or uploaded certificates and private keys, and Kerberos and NTLM-encrypted traffic using domain keys from Active Directory. The documentation says decrypted payloads are not written to disk. The vendor's site also describes fingerprinting of traffic that is not decrypted.
Detections carry risk scores and are flagged when recommended for triage, a MITRE map view groups them by technique, and Smart Investigations automatically group related detections into a timeline.
Transaction records and continuous packet capture can be searched and packets downloaded. Full packet capture needs the Packet Forensics module and a packet store.

The product is passive and does not block traffic itself. The documentation covers containing a device through CrowdStrike Falcon from a detection, and integrations with SIEM and SOAR products including Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, IBM QRadar, Google Security Operations and Cortex XSOAR.

encryption.value: Systems connect to the vendor's cloud services over an encrypted connection, and the documentation says decrypted traffic payloads are not written to disk. products.description: Run-time security layer that inspects prompts and responses between applications or agents and AI models and applies customer-defined policies to block prompt injection, jailbreaks, sensitive-data disclosure and harmful output. It is the former CalypsoAI product (previously named Inference Defend), acquired by F5 in September 2025, and is sold alongside the separate F5 AI Red Team product within the F5 AI Security Platform. independentTests.result: SecureIQLab, engaged by F5, ran 19,679 adversarial payloads across 10 threat categories; F5 reports 19,356 blocked, a security score of 98.36%, with category scores including prompt injection 99.33%, sensitive data leakage 99.01%, excessive agency 98.68% and toxic output 99.72%. F5's report page gives a lower 95.7% for unsafe outputs. The figures were read on F5's pages, published 2026-03-23; the tester's own report was not found on its site and its date is not stated. No other vendor was tested.

support.note: The product terms say edge deployments inherit the DDoS defences of Fastly's network and Cloud WAF deployments mitigate protocol floods such as SYN floods and UDP, DNS, NTP and SSDP reflection. The firewall itself inspects only HTTP and HTTPS. Protection of non-web network traffic is the separate Fastly Network Protect product, which applies firewall rules set in advance and does not detect attacks automatically.

Rate limiting and attack thresholds are part of the firewall. Fastly DDoS Protection, which detects and mitigates application-layer floods automatically, is included in the Core Plus and Total packages and is an add-on otherwise; it needs a paid Fastly delivery or Compute account.

Standard API signals are in every package. API Discovery is included in the Total package and an add-on otherwise; it works on sampled traffic and is built for REST APIs. API Enforcement, which validates requests against an uploaded schema, is a separate purchase and is not available for Compute services.

Basic bot detection is part of the firewall. The Bot Management product (client fingerprinting, challenges, headless-browser detection) is included in the Total package and an add-on otherwise, and must be bought with Fastly's delivery product.

Fastly Client-Side Protection inventories page resources and enforces content security policies; it requires the Next-Gen WAF, is included in the Core Plus and Total packages and relies on browser support for content security policy headers.

Fastly DDoS Protection watches each service's traffic and writes its own mitigation rules during an attack without manual tuning. The firewall's own attack thresholds are defaults that the customer raises or lowers; no per-application learning of firewall rules is documented.

products.description: Secrets security platform that finds hardcoded credentials (API keys, tokens, passwords, certificates) in source repositories and their history, CI/CD pipelines, container and package registries, collaboration tools and developer machines, checks whether each is still valid, and manages the resulting incidents through to revocation. It also monitors public GitHub for an organisation's leaked credentials, inventories non-human identities across vaults and cloud identity services, and plants decoy credentials (honeytokens). The ggshield command-line tool blocks secrets before commit or push and in AI coding tools. It is sold as a hosted service in US or EU regions or self-hosted on Kubernetes. It does not analyse code for vulnerabilities, scan dependencies or test running applications.

independentTests.result: Artificial Analysis benchmarks six open-weight model endpoints served by Groq. Time to first answer token ranged from 1.22 seconds (gpt-oss-120b, low reasoning) to 7.52 seconds, blended prices from US$0.05 to US$0.20 per million tokens, and error rates from 0.0% to 6.7%. products.description: Protection for Android and iOS apps and SDKs. DexGuard (Android) and iXGuard (iOS) are build-time tools that obfuscate and encrypt an app's code and insert runtime self-protection checks; they run in the customer's own build environment. ThreatCast is a hosted console that receives detections from protected apps in the field, and App Attestation is a hosted service that lets a back end check that calls come from a genuine, untampered app. The three are sold together in plans named Core, Control and Command. This record does not cover AppSweep, the vendor's mobile app security testing product, the XTD products bought from Verimatrix in February 2026, which are still sold and supported under their own name, or the Runway and Bugfender products whose acquisition was announced in November 2026.

products.description: Identity-based secrets management product. It stores and distributes secrets, issues short-lived dynamic credentials, rotates static and root credentials, manages certificates and keys, and offers encryption as a service, with access controlled by policy for people, machines and services. It is available as a free Community edition, a licensed self-managed Enterprise edition, and HCP Vault Dedicated, a hosted service run on AWS or Azure. IBM, which has owned HashiCorp since February 2025, also lists it as IBM Vault in its pricing and compliance material.

auditTrails.value: Audit entries can be written to file, syslog or socket devices, with most string values stored as HMAC-SHA256 hashes that can be compared through an API. If no enabled audit device can record a request, Vault refuses it. HCP Vault Dedicated keeps audit logs available for download for 30 days. No tamper-evidence mechanism is described on the pages reviewed.

logging.value: Audit devices record all API requests and responses in detail; a short list of system endpoints is exempt. Auditing must be enabled on a new self-managed cluster and is on by default in HCP Vault Dedicated. Server process logs are separate from audit logs.

siemIntegration.value: Documented streaming destinations for HCP Vault Dedicated audit logs include Splunk, Datadog and Elasticsearch; self-managed clusters can send audit logs by syslog or socket.

telemetryExport.value: HCP Vault Dedicated streams audit logs and metrics to CloudWatch, Datadog, Elasticsearch, Grafana Cloud, an HTTP sink, New Relic and Splunk (not on Development tier clusters). Self-managed Vault writes audit logs to file, syslog or socket for collection by the customer's tooling.

Vault-related entries were an HCP Vault cluster update and creation incident on Azure (9 October 2026), a degraded scanning incident for HCP Vault Radar (16 September 2026) and emergency maintenance for HCP Vault Radar (15 November 2026), all marked resolved. No formal post-incident reviews were linked in the feed.

supportModel.value: From the April 2026 2.x release, Vault Enterprise follows IBM's Support Cycle-2: two years of base support, one year of critical extended support and three years of sustained support per major release. Earlier long-term-support releases keep their terms (1.19.x maintenance ends April 2027). The vendor said in August 2025 that its support systems would align with IBM Support with equivalent plans. Response-time targets were not found on the pages reviewed.
