Exploitability score per asset using CVSS metrics, enterprise risk score, threat-level and business-impact scores from weighted attributes (including data classification), and classification of assets as PQC-safe or PQC-unsafe.
The proxy component's documentation lists ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and the FIPS 205 hash-based signature scheme; default TLS groups include ML-KEM-512/768/1024.

Default TLS groups include the hybrids X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024, with classical groups as fallback. The documentation says TLS 1.3 is required for post-quantum key exchange.

The Adaptive Proxy applies quantum-safe TLS in front of applications without application changes, and Proxy Manager can push selective configuration updates to proxies. Cryptography Manager policies are detective only: the documentation says they do not prevent creation or use of non-conforming assets.

independentTests.result: Bishop Fox, engaged by Illumio, ran emulated ransomware attacks against a Windows test environment in March and April 2022 with one consultant attacking and one defending. With no segmentation the attacker compromised all hosts in about 2.5 hours; with detection and response only the attack was contained in 38 minutes; with pre-configured static policy in 24 minutes; with full application ring-fencing by Illumio Core in 10 minutes, the attacker not moving beyond the first host. This was a single-vendor test with no competitors, so there is no rank. Press coverage noted the limits: few attack styles, a Windows-only environment and a two-person team.

independentTests.result: iBeta lists a Level 3 presentation attack detection confirmation letter for Incode Deepsight v1.0 on Android and iOS, meaning the tested version passed iBeta's ISO/IEC 30107-3 test at that level. iBeta's list shows passes only, the vendor chooses what to submit, and the letter itself was not opened in this pass.

iBeta lists a Level 2 presentation attack detection confirmation letter for Incode Omni 1.0, meaning the tested version passed iBeta's ISO/IEC 30107-3 test at that level. iBeta's list shows passes only, the vendor chooses what to submit, and the letter itself was not opened in this pass.

NIST lists the face-matching algorithm incode-016 from Incode Technologies, submitted 2026-09-30. False non-match rates, with NIST's rank among the 457 algorithms in the table read in brackets: mugshot 0.0021 (7), mugshot with 12 or more years between photos 0.0022 (20), visa to border 0.0019 (16), visa to border at 45 degrees or more of head turn 0.0055 (12), border 0.0038 (17), border to kiosk 0.0469 (37). Lower is better. NIST tests the developer's algorithm and does not name the commercial product, so this is evidence about the face matcher inside the product, not the whole product.

ID Tech reported on 2026-03-31 that Incode was one of five of the 16 systems tested that met all of the US Department of Homeland Security's performance goals for matching a selfie to an identity document, in a test with 1,632 volunteers. No figures for Incode are given. The department publishes results under anonymous labels, so the attribution to Incode rests on the company's own disclosure as relayed by the article.

support.note: Infisical is software and does not provide hardware key storage. Self-hosted Enterprise instances can wrap the root key with an external PKCS#11 HSM (Thales Luna, AWS CloudHSM and Fortanix are named).
The KMS creates and stores keys and performs encrypt, decrypt, sign, verify and MAC operations through the UI, API and a KMIP server, with key rotation and import and export.

A customer can protect its Infisical project keys with its own AWS KMS or Google Cloud KMS key, and KMIP clients such as storage arrays can keep their keys in Infisical. Supplying customer-held keys to third-party cloud services is not described.

Enterprise customers can run a FIPS image that the vendor says uses FIPS 140-3 validated cryptographic modules. The module and its certificate number are not named in the documentation; an attestation letter is said to be in the trust centre, which could not be read.

support.note: The API reference lists streams of forum posts, forum private messages, messaging-service messages, data-leak-site posts and marketplace listings. The vendor says these come from its own researchers engaging with actors and from automated collection across forums, marketplaces and messaging groups.

The finished intelligence data sheet lists the report types written by the vendor's analysts (breach reports, quarterly threat briefs, malware campaign reports, profile reports and others); the API exposes them as finished-intelligence, information, spot, malware, vulnerability and geopolitical reports.

Profile reports cover an actor, marketplace or service with identifiers and tactics, techniques and procedures; the API has actor and malware-family endpoints. The data sheet says reporting is aligned with MITRE ATT&CK, and the AI Assistant is described as extracting ATT&CK technique tables from reports. A published technique mapping for each profile was not seen.

The API's indicator model carries a confidence score from 0 to 100, an expiry time, kill-chain phases and the linked malware family for IP address, domain, URL, email and file indicators; reports carry an Admiralty code for source reliability. support.note: An agent authors a patch scoped to one confirmed finding from the platform's static analysis or pentest. Patching starts only when a user selects the finding.

The platform re-runs the scanner that raised the finding on the affected files, or replays the stored exploit against the patched target. After a bounded number of retries a patch that does not verify is not delivered and a failure reason is shown. Before-and-after scanner output and the diff are attached.

Patches arrive as pull requests on GitHub Cloud and Enterprise Cloud and Azure DevOps and as merge requests on GitLab (all hosting modes). GitHub Enterprise Server is listed as roadmap. Scans run from CI and can gate builds on exploited findings.

Remediation covers findings from Keygraph's own agentic static analysis and pentests. No page read describes importing findings from third-party scanners, and no list of supported programming languages was found.
The Code Remediation page lists remediation for dependency (SCA) and secrets findings as roadmap and not available yet. Configuration fixes are not mentioned.

Patching is user-initiated only; patches are never auto-applied and the platform does not commit to protected branches. Write access to repositories is requested only when Code Remediation is enabled. Each patch is limited to one finding and attributed to a labelled bot. Role-based permissions per project, scanner and finding action are described on the Enterprise page. No setting that restricts which files or change types a patch may touch was found.

Enterprise runs entirely in the customer's environment, including air-gapped with a local model. Every edition uses the customer's own model key. The terms of service commit to no training of shared models on customer content. In the cloud edition the full source tree is not persisted.

independentTests.result: Mistral Large 4 scored 26 on the Intelligence Index, 31st of 69 scored models; the leader scored 65. Mistral Medium 3.5 scored 5 and Mistral Small 4 scored 4.

Different, and the difference is large. The best-placed Mistral model is Mistral Medium 3.5 at 127th with 1,426, followed by Mistral Large 4 at 134th with 1,423. Mistral Medium 3.1 is 164th with 1,408, as recorded, but it is not the best-placed Mistral model, and Mistral Large 4 does have a rank.

products.description: NVIDIA's customer-facing AI cloud platform: a managed layer for development pods, batch jobs and inference endpoints that runs on GPU capacity from NVIDIA cloud partners or on the customer's own compute, with serverless endpoints and NIM microservices reached through build.nvidia.com. NVIDIA now describes DGX Cloud itself mainly as its internal cloud, still sold to enterprises by private offer on the large cloud marketplaces. The May 2025 launch offered early access; no later general-availability statement was found. Press reported in April 2025 that the platform derives from NVIDIA's purchase of the start-up Lepton AI.
products.name: NVIDIA DGX Cloud Lepton

logging.value: The documentation lists built-in observability as a platform feature alongside storage; no detail page on logs or metrics was found.

cloudProviders.note: The first ten are the cloud partners named at launch in May 2025 as marketplace suppliers; the last four are named as sub-processors in the Cloud Services DPA. The current partner list was not found.

exitAndSubstitutability.value: The Cloud Agreement states NVIDIA will not retain customer data for retrieval after termination and advises customers to keep their own backups; the DPA commits to deletion within 90 days. The platform runs on capacity from several cloud partners or the customer's own Kubernetes, and endpoints serve open models through vLLM or NIM containers that can also be self-hosted. No exit assistance is described.

supportModel.value: Support cases are filed through the NVIDIA Enterprise Support Portal under an entitlement arranged by a technical account manager. The enterprise support policy defines Standard, Critical and Premium tiers, with initial response targets for severity 1 of 4 business hours (Standard) or 1 hour (Critical and Premium) and round-the-clock cover for severity 1 and 2 on the higher tiers. Which tier applies to Lepton is not stated.

regulatoryMappings.statement: Supports the bank in documenting processor terms for personal data through a cloud services data processing addendum that applies EU standard contractual clauses, gives 30 days' notice of new sub-processors and commits to deletion within 90 days of termination.

opportunities.point: The agreed acquisition of Hugging Face could widen the catalogue and reach of NVIDIA's hosted model services.

strengths.point: Very strong vendor finances: US$65.3B net income in the latest quarter.
Workloads can run on several cloud partners or on the customer's own compute, and models served through NIM can be self-hosted.
Published enterprise support policy with severity definitions and response targets.

threats.point: Abrupt chief executive resignation in November 2026 with an interim successor.
Export controls and competition inquiries in several jurisdictions, as disclosed in the 10-K.
NVIDIA has repositioned DGX Cloud as an internal environment, which shows its cloud offerings can change direction.

weaknesses.point: Little public documentation of security attestations, audit logging, regions or service levels for this product.
The Cloud Agreement gives no audit rights and no data retrieval after termination.
The cloud platform is a small, undisclosed part of NVIDIA's business and is not mentioned in its latest results release.

support.note: Fine-tunes a language model on the customer's table and generates new records with no one-to-one mapping to the originals; numeric, categorical, text and temporal columns are supported.
Each job reports a Data Privacy Score built from simulated membership inference and attribute inference attacks, and separately counts personal data replayed from the training set.
Optional DP-SGD training with a configurable epsilon (default 8) and delta, off by default. The documentation says it works best with 10,000 or more records and slows training by two to four times.
Detects personal data with a dedicated model, language-model classification and regular expressions, then replaces, redacts or hashes it before synthesis.
Outside the product's stated scope: the overview describes synthetic data generation and personal-data replacement, not computation on encrypted or partitioned data.

In the standalone Docker set-up, personal-data classification defaults to a remote NVIDIA inference endpoint unless the customer points it elsewhere.

products.description: Open-source tool that creates synthetic versions of sensitive tabular datasets. It detects and replaces personal data, fine-tunes a language model on the customer's table, optionally with differential privacy, generates new records, and reports quality and privacy scores. It runs on the customer's own NVIDIA GPUs, alone or as part of the NeMo Helix platform. NVIDIA's container catalog describes it as an early access release.
products.name: NVIDIA NeMo Safe Synthesizer

auditorEvidence.note: The report is produced by the tool itself; no independent validation of its privacy scores was found.
auditorEvidence.value: The per-job evaluation report, available as HTML and JSON, documents the quality and privacy scores of each synthetic dataset and whether personal data from the training set reappears in it.

explainability.value: The evaluation report breaks the Synthetic Quality Score and Data Privacy Score into named components, such as column distribution stability and membership inference protection, with charts comparing training and synthetic data.

logging.value: Each job stores its results, including an HTML evaluation report and a JSON summary with scores and timings. When run in NeMo Helix on Kubernetes, the platform emits OpenTelemetry traces and metrics.

telemetryExport.value: NeMo Helix exports traces and metrics over OTLP to a collector the customer runs, configured in the Helm chart. Evaluation results are available as JSON through the SDK.

cloudProviders.reason: Self-hosted software: the documentation describes running it on the customer's own machines or Kubernetes cluster.

dataProcessingLocations.reason: Self-hosted software: the documentation describes running it on the customer's own machines or Kubernetes cluster. Processing takes place where the customer deploys it.

exitAndSubstitutability.value: The source code is published under the Apache 2.0 licence and outputs are ordinary tabular data, so a customer can keep running the version it has. NVIDIA's container catalog states that the NeMo microservices packaging, in which the tool was first distributed, was sunset on 2026-10-01 with no further releases; current documentation is under NeMo Helix, at version 0.11.

incidentHistory.reason: Self-hosted software: the documentation describes running it on the customer's own machines or Kubernetes cluster. There is no vendor-run service whose outages could be recorded.

modelProviders.note: Personal-data detection uses NVIDIA's own Nemotron model. The base language models that are fine-tuned are not named in the documentation read; the Docker guide shows them being downloaded from Hugging Face and mentions gated Llama and Mistral model families as examples.

supportModel.value: NVIDIA's container catalog describes NeMo Safe Synthesizer as an early access release with limited support and possible API changes, and says production use of the container needs an NVIDIA AI Enterprise licence. The NeMo Helix governing terms page places the source code under the Apache 2.0 licence and does not mention support.

opportunities.point: Sits within NeMo Helix alongside NVIDIA's evaluation, guardrail and anonymisation tools, so it can be adopted as part of a wider toolkit.

strengths.point: Documents five of the six category capabilities, including differential privacy with stated parameters and attack-based privacy scoring.
Open source under Apache 2.0 and run entirely on the customer's own infrastructure.
Backed by a highly profitable listed vendor.

threats.point: Usage telemetry is on by default, and one set-up path defaults to a remote NVIDIA endpoint for classifying personal data.

NVIDIA's own catalogue says NeMo microservices, the packaging tracked here, were sunset on 1 October 2026 with no new releases. NVIDIA still publishes Safe Synthesizer containers under newer platform names with no notice, and does not explain how they relate, so the product's future form should be confirmed with NVIDIA.

weaknesses.point: Described by NVIDIA as early access with limited support; platform documentation versions are still below 1.0.
Needs a data-centre NVIDIA GPU with at least 40 GB of memory on Linux.
No audit trail or SIEM integration is documented.

Application-to-application retrieval gives applications credentials through an API. auditTrails.value: Access requests, approvals, reviews, password changes and sessions are recorded. Audit log archives are hashed with SHA-256 and signed with the cluster's audit log signing certificate. Session audit trails can be digitally signed and timestamped at a configurable interval and encrypted. Audit log purge and archive to an archive server are scheduled by the administrator; the guide recommends keeping no more than six months on the appliance.

auditorEvidence.value: Built-in audit, access-request and secrets reports export to JSON or CSV; signed audit log archives and signed, timestamped session recordings can be verified outside the product. For the vendor's own controls, a SOC 3 report and ISO/IEC 27001 certificate are public on the trust centre, and SOC 1 Type II and SOC 2 Type II reports, a bridge letter and penetration-test summaries for the Passwords and Sessions modules are available on request.

explainability.value: Access request policies can require the requester to give a comment and a predefined reason code, and the reviewer to comment; emergency access that bypasses approval is flagged and can notify a contact list. Reports list requests by requester, approver and reviewer, and auto-approved requests. How the analytics module explains the risk scores it assigns was not found in the pages read.

logging.value: Safeguard for Privileged Passwords records an audit log that can be queried in the web client and API, forwarded to syslog servers by event subscription, and archived on a schedule. Safeguard for Privileged Sessions records every proxied session as an audit trail file and forwards session events to SIEM systems.

siemIntegration.value: The universal SIEM forwarder is documented for Splunk (6.5 or later, JSON-CIM) and, through CEF, ArcSight ESM, IBM QRadar and Microsoft Azure Sentinel. Safeguard On Demand manages forwarding destinations for both modules in one page.

telemetryExport.value: Passwords audit events are sent to syslog servers in CEF or JSON, by event subscription; session data is sent as RFC 3164 syslog messages with a JSON, CEF or JSON-CIM body, optionally over TLS. Reports export to JSON or CSV, and audit data can be read through the REST API. The session forwarder does not send historical data.

support.note: Registration rules decide which authentication methods a customer may or must enrol, and identity proofing can be called during a flow through a Photo ID method that relies on Jumio's Netverify service, or a custom third-party check. The product does not itself sign customers up or collect profile attributes: it stores authenticator data and sits behind the bank's own application, which holds the customer record.

Synced and device-bound passkeys, FIDO UAF and FIDO2/WebAuthn, device biometrics and security keys are documented, with autofill of passkeys in the browser. Biometric Update reported in 2018 that the FIDO Alliance certified the predecessor S3 Authentication Suite for FIDO2.

Adaptive authentication rules compare context data, signals and user history (for example location, registered authenticators, time since last sign-in and the transaction) and return allow, deny or trigger authentication with a required sequence of methods. Smart Sense, an adjunct product, analyses typical user behaviour.

The documentation describes transactions as cryptographic proof of a user's confirmation of specific transaction details, with a transaction confirmation token, push approval out of band and support for the Secure Payment Confirmation web standard.

Registration, authentication and recovery behaviour is set in adaptive rulesets and FIDO policies held on the server and edited in the Admin Console, per tenant, so the decisions are not hard-coded in each web, iOS or Android app; API server plugins and replaceable SDK screens allow the bank's own logic and interface. It is rule-based configuration; no visual flow designer is described in the pages read.

Account recovery is documented through adaptive authentication: a customer who loses or replaces a device can regain access with email or SMS one-time codes, Photo ID, or a previously registered alternative authenticator such as a security key, and an existing device can be used to approve a new one (device blessing). The recovery screens are part of the bank's own app.

Outside the product's stated scope: the server documentation describes storing authenticator-related data (authenticator metadata, key IDs and user public keys), not customer profiles with custom attributes or a record of consents. No profile or consent management page appears in the documentation index.

auditTrails.value: Audit logs are tamper-evident: each line is written with a checksum, and a command-line verifier reports any altered log. Logged events include client registration, authentication, deletion and transactions, and administrator changes to server properties, policies and metadata. The verifier does not work on the CSV-format runtime log.

auditorEvidence.value: The audit log verification command lets a customer show that audit logs were not altered after they were written; the documentation says the tamper-evident logging is designed to meet regulatory requirements. logging.value: Four audit logs are documented, kept per tenant: a runtime audit log of user registrations and authentications in JSON, the same in a CSV-like format for the Insights and Smart Sense add-ons, an Admin Console audit log and a command-line tool audit log. Diagnostic logs and access logs are configurable separately. Runtime audit logs roll over at 100 MB or daily and are compressed.

products.description: Palo Alto Networks' endpoint protection and extended detection and response product, announced on 26 February 2019 and available to customers from 4 March 2019. independentTests.result: Cortex XDR Prevent 9.1 was one of 11 Certified Leaders among 14 products: 98.0% active response, 98.0% passive response and 98.0% combined, with low operational-accuracy costs and a modelled five-year operational impact of $1,243 per agent. Cortex XDR Prevent 8.8 was certified with 99.3% active response, 98.7% passive response and 99.0% combined, at a modelled five-year cost of $882 per agent; three of the ten named products scored higher on the combined measure.

support.note: Expander discovers new, existing and unknown internet-facing assets (IP ranges, certificates, domains, cloud resources, websites and services) and attributes them to the organisation.

The Attack Surface Testing add-on runs benign exploits against externally facing services, with the customer's approval, and marks each as confirmed vulnerable or confirmed not vulnerable, showing the evidence payload the service returned.

Outside the product's stated scope: the documentation overview describes asset discovery, rules, single-service vulnerability tests and response playbooks, and does not describe linking weaknesses into a route to a sensitive system.
Outside the product's stated scope: Xpanse works from the public internet on internet-facing assets and is agentless; testing inside the network or of directory and identity systems is not described.

Websites are inventoried and tests run against externally facing services matched by service type, for CVEs and other risks such as default credentials. The pages read do not describe testing of web application flaw classes or of APIs.

Exploits run only with the customer's approval; targets can be all directly discovered services or a selected subset; each test carries an intrusivity level from 0 to 5 and more intrusive tests are optional; individual tests can be disabled. Automated remediation is limited to non-production assets by default.

Test results carry remediation guidance; Active Response playbooks can restrict ports, patch or isolate, and finish with a remediation confirmation scan; release 2.14 added an on-demand rescan from a testing alert.

products.description: Palo Alto Networks' external attack surface management service, built on the technology of Expanse, acquired in December 2020. Its main application, Expander, is a cloud service and API that scans the public internet, attributes internet-facing assets to the customer and raises alerts on risky exposures. Two add-ons extend it: Attack Surface Testing runs benign exploits against the customer's externally facing services to confirm vulnerabilities, and Active Response runs playbooks that route and remediate exposures. The Form 10-K for fiscal 2026 describes it as offered both as a stand-alone cloud service and as a subscription module within Cortex XSIAM. It does not test inside the network.

support.note: Discovery is from network sessions seen by the vendor's firewalls and Prisma Access (TLS, SSH and VPN tunnels: protocols, key exchange, algorithms, certificates), with host context such as library and operating-system versions added through optional connectors to tools such as Qualys, CrowdStrike, Splunk and ServiceNow. Scanning of source code, binaries or cloud key stores is not described, and decryption policy and handshake logging must be configured first.

The inventory is described as a dynamic cryptographic bill of materials inside the application. The only export documented is a PDF report that can be shared or scheduled; no structured or standard-format inventory export was found.

Each asset is placed in one of three risk categories (deprecated cryptography, harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure, quantum-secure) and ranked using a business-impact rating set by rule or by hand, quantum readiness, and the volume of data in transit. No numeric scoring method is published.

PAN-OS documentation lists ML-KEM in its standard post-quantum decryption option, and cipher translation re-encrypts with ML-KEM. These run in PAN-OS 12.1 and later on the firewall, not in the application itself. Support for the NIST signature standards was not found on the pages read.
Documentation says cipher translation uses hybrid post-quantum key exchange, and PAN-OS supports hybrid IKEv2 key exchange under RFC 9370 for site-to-site VPNs from 11.2.

Algorithms are changed through decryption profiles and security policy on the firewall, pushed by a guided wizard, without changing the applications behind it; PAN-OS 12.1 lists a crypto-agility feature. This applies only to traffic that passes through the vendor's firewalls or Prisma Access, and the product page says profile updates are made by the administrator.

Documentation says PKI managers can be connected as optional data sources for certificate inventory. Integration with hardware security modules or certificate authorities for issuing or rotating keys is not described.

The NIST CMVP list of active validations for Palo Alto Networks, read on 2026-11-21, includes PAN-OS 10.1, 10.2, 11.1 and 11.2 but no PAN-OS 12 module, and no module name refers to post-quantum algorithms; the post-quantum decryption and cipher translation features require PAN-OS 12.1. auditorEvidence.value: Executive reports on cryptographic risk can be generated, scheduled and shared as PDF. The vendor's launch post says the product audits the environment against NIST, FIPS 140-3 and DORA; the documentation read refers only to NIST and describes no framework mapping.

explainability.value: For each asset the application shows the cryptography in use, traces weak cryptography to a cause such as an old library or operating-system version, and names the decryption profiles and policy rules that permit the weak sessions.

logging.value: The application works from SSL/TLS and SSH decryption logs, traffic logs and tunnel inspection logs that firewalls and Prisma Access forward to Strata Logging Service; it shows the past 24 hours, 7 days or 30 days.

siemIntegration.value: No outbound integration of the inventory or risk findings with a SIEM was found. The underlying decryption and traffic logs can be forwarded from Strata Logging Service to Microsoft Sentinel, Splunk, Exabeam and Google Chronicle, and the application can take in data from Splunk and other tools as sources.

telemetryExport.value: Reports can be generated from the overview or inventory, downloaded as PDF, shared and scheduled. The underlying logs can be forwarded from Strata Logging Service in standard formats. No API or structured export of the inventory was found.

dataProcessingLocations.note: The table read does not name the Quantum-Safe Security application; this assumes it is processed with Strata Cloud Manager, which the documentation says hosts it.
value: Follows the customer's Strata Logging Service region; Strata Cloud Manager is processed in the United Kingdom, Germany, Switzerland, Singapore, India, Japan, Canada, United States, Australia or Qatar depending on that region

exitAndSubstitutability.value: The application reads logs the customer's firewalls already produce, so stopping it does not change traffic handling; the inventory can be taken away only as PDF reports. Cipher translation is different: sessions re-encrypted at the firewall depend on PAN-OS 12.1 or later staying in the path, so replacing the firewalls removes that protection for legacy systems.

incidentHistory.value: The vendor's status feed, read on 2026-11-21, showed no entries naming Strata Cloud Manager or Strata Logging Service, on which the application depends, between September and November 2026. Quantum-Safe Security was not seen as a named component. Earlier history was not read.

supportModel.value: The Form 10-K says level-three support is delivered around the clock from regional support centres located worldwide, with channel partners that run authorised support centres typically handling the first two levels. The launch post also offers a quantum readiness assessment and professional services with partners. No Quantum-Safe Security-specific support tiers or response-time commitments were found on the pages retrieved.

standardsMappings.statement: Supports the bank in moving sessions to the key-encapsulation mechanism standardised in FIPS 203, because firewalls running PAN-OS 12.1 or later can negotiate ML-KEM and re-encrypt classical sessions from systems that cannot be upgraded.

Supports the bank in reviewing the cryptography in use against FIPS 140-3 expectations, which the vendor's launch post names as a framework the product audits against; the documentation read does not describe that mapping.

opportunities.point: The vendor's installed base of firewalls gives it a ready route to market, and the launch post planned further integrations for April 2026.
SDxCentral reports that Gartner credited the vendor's post-quantum enhancements in its 2026 SASE evaluation.

strengths.point: Uses firewalls and Prisma Access tenants already deployed as sensors, so discovery needs no new agents or appliances.
Cipher translation lets legacy and IoT systems that cannot be upgraded have their sessions re-encrypted with post-quantum key exchange at the firewall.
Asset views trace weak cryptography to the library, operating system and policy rule responsible.

threats.point: The product has been available for under a year and CSO Online's coverage relied on company statements, with no independent assessment.
Cipher translation ties quantum-safe protection of legacy systems to keeping this vendor's firewalls in the traffic path.

weaknesses.point: Discovery is limited to traffic the vendor's own firewalls and Prisma Access see, and needs decryption policy and handshake logging to be configured.
The inventory can be exported only as PDF reports; no structured cryptographic bill of materials export is documented.
No CMVP-validated module was listed for PAN-OS 12, which carries the post-quantum features.
No customers were named in the launch material or in CSO Online's report.

support.note: Detects cloned and AI-generated speech in files and on live calls, without enrolling a voiceprint; the Help Center lists three audio models whose signals are combined into one score. Podonos, a voice AI evaluation company, tested the audio detector on 4,524 English clips: 71.3% accuracy, with 53.7% of genuine recordings flagged at the shipping threshold and clips under 1.5 seconds left unscored. Its later round placed the product seventh of 16 systems. Podonos has worked commercially with Resemble AI, the top-scoring vendor in the first round.

Detects generated or manipulated images and video. The Help Center lists image models for diffusion, face swaps, GANs and visual noise, applied to the full image and to faces, and video models applied to full frames and faces. A Purdue University study of nine commercial tools on images from real political deepfake incidents reported the product's image detector at 93.51% accuracy, the highest of the nine, with a 5.53% false-alarm rate; one other tool had a higher AUC and one a lower false-alarm rate. Its video detector was not in that study.

RealCall analyses the caller's audio in short overlapping segments during the call and delivers results progressively through the Session API and webhooks; release notes record a time-to-conclusion field and the API reference has a segments endpoint to poll while a call is in progress. RealMeeting scans participant audio and video during a meeting and shows the organiser a result in a side panel. No latency figure is published. Podonos measured the file-analysis audio detector as slower than real time (real-time factor 1.52); that test did not cover RealCall.

The product scores the content of media and does not inspect the capture channel. The vendor's IDmission case study describes an AI-generated selfie that was injected by file upload and API submission: the product flagged the image as generated from its pixel patterns, and the same page describes injection detection at the capture layer, which checks that an image came from a camera sensor on a trusted device, as a separate control for the verification platform to run. No virtual camera, emulator or injected audio detection is described on the product, solution or Help Center pages read.

Contact centre: RealCall takes call audio by SIPREC from a session border controller, with tested profiles for Oracle and Ribbon controllers and Twilio, and release notes refer to Genesys and Amazon Connect integrations. Meetings: RealMeeting for Microsoft Teams was announced in November 2026 and is installed from Microsoft's marketplace; i-SCOOP reports that RealMeeting also covers Zoom, and the vendor's product page refers the reader to documentation for the current list. Identity verification: Fintech Finance News reported in July 2026 that AU10TIX takes the product's detection signal into its onboarding risk scoring. Setup guides for Genesys and Amazon Connect were not read.

Two parties other than the vendor have tested and published its accuracy. A Purdue University study (arXiv, October 2025) reported the image detector at 93.51% accuracy, 95.82% AUC and a 5.53% false-alarm rate on images from real political deepfake incidents. Podonos reported the audio detector at 71.3% accuracy with 53.7% of genuine English recordings flagged. The vendor publishes no accuracy figures on the pages read, and no independent test of its video detector, RealCall or RealMeeting was found.

Results give a score from 0 to 100, a conclusion band (Authentic, Suspicious, Manipulated), indicators of which detection models were triggered, and a plain-language reason when a scan is inconclusive; the Help Center says what to do for each band. RealCall shows which call segments drove the result, with audio playback. The AWS Marketplace listing describes heatmaps, timelines, face boxes and waveforms showing where manipulation is most likely, and PDF or CSV reports. The model indicators name a class of technique, not the specific evidence in the file.

products.description: Deepfake detection platform that scores audio, video and images for signs of AI generation or manipulation. It is sold as four products: RealAPI for files submitted by an application, RealScan for browser review, RealCall for live phone calls and RealMeeting for virtual meetings. It analyses the media itself and returns a score with supporting detail; it does not verify identity and does not check whether media was injected into a capture channel, so banks and identity verification providers add its findings to their own controls.

independentTests.result: Ranked 7th of 16 detectors and last of 7 commercial services: 71.27% accuracy, with a 53.7% false-positive rate (real speech flagged as fake) and a 3.6% false-negative rate. Latency was 5,718 ms, the only system slower than real time. It was scored on 3,745 of the 4,524 clips because it rejects short clips. The post itself carries no date.

support.note: FLAT, HNSW and SVS-VAMANA index types; L2, inner product and cosine distance; k-nearest-neighbour and range queries; float and 8-bit integer vector types; a per-shard result ratio for clustered deployments. Vector sets add a native data type with 8-bit and binary quantisation. Compression using Intel's proprietary optimisations is not available in Redis Open Source.

FT.HYBRID (Redis 8.4 and later) fuses BM25 text search and vector similarity by reciprocal rank fusion or a weighted linear combination; it is supported on Redis Software and Redis Cloud but not on Flex databases. Earlier versions combine vector search with text, tag, numeric and geo filters in one query.

Access control lists and database roles restrict users by command, key pattern and pub/sub channel. A user can create or read a search index only with access to a superset of the index's key prefixes, and FT.HYBRID returns only keys the user can read. No per-document or per-attribute policy on search results is documented, so tenant separation relies on key naming and separate indexes or databases.
Redis Software and Redis Open Source both include Redis Search and run on customer infrastructure.

Redis 8 and later, including the search engine, are offered under AGPLv3 as well as the source-available RSALv2 and SSPLv1. Versions 7.4 to 7.8 were source-available only, and 7.2 and earlier were BSD-licensed. Some vector compression optimisations are reserved for the commercial products.

Redis Cloud Pro subscriptions can use a customer-held key in AWS KMS or Google Cloud KMS for persistent storage; Azure and Essentials plans are not mentioned, and data in memory is not covered by the page. Redis Software relies on file-system encryption that the customer configures.

customerDataTrainsModels.note: The LangCache documentation states that Redis does not access customer data or use it to train AI models. The Redis Cloud Agreement, as read, licenses customer data only as needed to provide the service and lets Redis use statistical usage data to improve it; it has no separate statement on model training. Vector search itself involves no vendor model.

customerManagedKeys.note: Redis Cloud Pro only, for persistent storage, with keys in AWS KMS or Google Cloud KMS. If the customer revokes the key, the database is deleted immediately or after a chosen grace period of 15 minutes to 24 hours, or kept in an alert-only mode in which the availability commitment does not apply.

encryption.note: Encryption covers persisted data on disk; the pages do not describe encryption of data held in memory.
encryption.value: Redis Cloud deployments are always encrypted at rest using the cloud provider's disk encryption (encrypted EBS and NVMe volumes on AWS, default disk encryption on Google Cloud and Azure), and TLS is available for connections. Redis Software does not encrypt data at rest itself and directs customers to Linux file-system encryption; it can encrypt its private keys on disk and supports TLS with configurable protocol versions.

products.description: The vector search capability of the Redis in-memory data store, sold as Redis Cloud (managed), Redis Software (self-managed) and available as Redis Open Source. Vectors are stored in hashes or JSON documents and indexed by Redis Search (previously called RediSearch and Redis Query Engine) with FLAT, HNSW or SVS-VAMANA indexes, with metadata filtering and, from Redis 8.4, a hybrid text-and-vector command. Redis 8 added a separate vector set data type. LangCache, a semantic caching service for model responses built on the same engine, is in preview. Vector similarity search became generally available in RediSearch 2.4 in March 2022. The vendor now also markets an agent-context layer called Redis Iris, which is not evaluated here.

auditTrails.value: Redis Software can audit database connections, authentication requests and individual commands, recording user, source address, command and key names but not values, and sends each record as JSON to a configured TCP listener. Auditing is off by default and delivery is best-effort: records can be dropped when the queue is full or the listener is unreachable, with metrics reporting the loss. Redis Cloud's system log records the originator and API key for each management activity; command-level auditing for Redis Cloud is not described in the pages read.

explainability.value: FT.HYBRID accepts an EXPLAINSCORE option (Redis 8.10 and later) that returns, for each result, how the combined score was computed from the text rank and the vector rank and the fusion parameters used.

logging.value: Redis Cloud keeps a system log of account, subscription and database activity that can be viewed in the console, exported as CSV or read through the GET /logs API. Redis Software logs management actions with who, what, when and outcome, viewable in the console or REST API and written to syslog; default rotation is daily or at 200 MB, keeping ten files for up to seven days, and is configurable.

siemIntegration.value: Redis Software's audit stream can be consumed by any TCP listener; the documentation names Imperva Sonar and IBM Guardium as examples and says no particular SIEM is required. Event logs can be forwarded by syslog. For Redis Cloud no SIEM connector is described beyond the logs API and CSV export.

telemetryExport.value: Redis Cloud Pro databases expose a Prometheus metrics endpoint, with Grafana dashboards published by the vendor; this is not available on Essentials plans. Redis Software exports metrics, writes its event log to syslog for forwarding, and streams audit records over TCP.

cloudProviders.note: For Redis Cloud the customer chooses the provider and region. Redis Software and Redis Open Source run on infrastructure of the customer's choosing.

Provided by Snowflake ML alongside Cortex: training on a container runtime, feature store, experiments, model registry, model serving, monitoring for drift, explainability and lineage. Cortex Agents call Cortex Analyst for SQL over structured data, Cortex Search for unstructured retrieval, custom stored procedures and functions, and tools on remote Model Context Protocol servers.

Cortex AI Guardrails screen for prompt injection and jailbreak attempts in Cortex Agents, CoWork and CoCo, in block or log-only mode. The vendor states that models run inside Snowflake's security and governance perimeter unless the customer elects otherwise, and private connectivity to the service over AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Link or Google Private Service Connect is available on Business Critical edition and above. The service runs in Snowflake's environment, not the customer's network, and most models are reached through cross-region inference.

Usage is billed in credits by token or page and recorded in account usage views with about five minutes' latency. Budgets and per-user quotas can limit agent and CoWork spend, and access is gated by database roles. The documented pattern for AI functions relies on customer-built alerts and tasks; the Cortex user role is granted to all users by default.

Agent evaluations run against a dataset with answer correctness, logical consistency and custom judged metrics, with runs compared side by side; tool selection and tool execution accuracy are in public preview. Custom applications can be evaluated through TruLens.

support.note: The API opens a pull request with an agent-authored fix for a finding; for code findings it patches the affected files.

The documentation describes retesting a finding to show whether it is still exploitable, and a retest scan that marks an open issue fixed when it no longer reproduces. The marketing page says fixes are retested before review and the pull request carries a validation summary; the documentation does not state that every fix pull request is retested before it is opened, and says AI-generated remediation needs human review.

Fix pull requests are opened in the connected repository; GitHub pull requests, GitLab merge requests and Bitbucket pull requests are accepted as a finding's fix PR, and Azure Repos can be connected. PR reviews run on pull requests through a GitHub App and report as a status check.

Fixes are generated for findings from Strix's own pentests, PR reviews and dependency scans. No import of findings from third-party scanners was found in the documentation, and no list of supported programming languages was found.

For dependency findings in npm-based projects the fix pull request bumps the direct dependency or pins the transitive package through npm, yarn or pnpm overrides. Other package ecosystems are not mentioned. The platform reports cloud and Kubernetes misconfigurations, but no automated fix for configuration findings is documented.

Fixes are delivered as pull requests for developer review, so merge control rests with the repository's own rules. When the chat agent tries to open a fix pull request, a member must approve the action first. Creating a fix PR needs a write-scoped token, and an administrator sets the title template and branch prefix. No policy that limits what a fix may change, or that forces review inside Strix, was found.

Enterprise can run in the customer's VPC, on-premises or air-gapped with the customer's own models, and the open-source agents run locally with self-hosted models. The privacy policy says customer data is not used to train or fine-tune AI models. On self-serve plans customer data may be used to evaluate and tune the vendor's prompts and agents unless the customer objects, and is processed by third-party model providers.

Sara AI agents attempt exploitation of external web applications and hosts and a human validates each finding before it is reported; findings carry replication steps and screenshots. Sara does not test internal assets, and sign-in flows protected by multi-factor codes are not supported.

The vendor says Sara maps attack paths and gives one example of three linked flaws exploited in sequence, and that researchers investigate chained weaknesses and lateral movement. No attack-path view or documented chaining feature was found.

Human researchers test internal networks over a VPN, covering segmentation, privilege escalation and lateral movement. Directory services such as Active Directory are not named, and Sara AI testing is external only.

Web application, API and mobile testing by researchers, and AI-led web testing for flaws such as injection, cross-site scripting and broken access control. The FedRAMP Marketplace entry describes testing of web, host, cloud, API, AI and mobile assets.

Assessments can be paused and resumed through the API or portal; researcher traffic goes through Synack's LaunchPoint gateway from known source addresses and is captured; Sara is limited to approved addresses, filters destructive commands and has findings checked by people.

Findings carry a severity score and fix recommendations; the customer requests patch verification in the portal or by API and a researcher retests and reports whether the fix worked. Patch verification is included in every tier.

support.note: The documentation lists twelve virtualisation platforms, Windows, Linux, AIX, Solaris and Mac computers, AWS, Azure and Google Cloud workloads, unstructured data, enterprise database plug-ins, MongoDB and Microsoft Entra ID. Microsoft 365 and Salesforce are protected by separate Veeam products with their own version numbers, so SaaS coverage inside this product is limited to Entra ID.

Backups can be made immutable for a set period on a hardened Linux repository, object storage, Dell Data Domain and HPE StoreOnce. The hardened repository is added with single-use credentials that are not stored on the backup server. Four-eyes authorisation can be required to delete backups or shorten immutability. Veeam Data Cloud Vault is an optional separately hosted immutable target.

Inline entropy analysis during backup flags encrypted files, onion links and ransom notes; file system activity analysis flags known suspicious files, mass deletions and extension changes. Affected workloads are marked Suspicious.
A Scan Backup session checks restore points with Veeam Threat Hunter signatures, third-party antivirus or YARA rules and finds the last clean restore point; Secure Restore scans during a restore.

The virtual lab is an isolated environment fenced off from production in which machines are started from backup for verification, sandbox testing and staged restore. Recovery Orchestrator documents a clean-room scenario that restores from an immutable copy at a remote site when the production backup server is unavailable. Virtual labs are documented for VMware vSphere and Hyper-V; Orchestrator's lab testing does not support Azure or Hyper-V recovery locations, and the clean-room scenario covers vSphere backups only.

Veeam Recovery Orchestrator builds recovery plans for applications, schedules readiness checks and tests in isolated labs, and produces reports for each check, test and execution. It is part of the Premium edition. SureBackup jobs in the base product verify recoverability on a schedule.

Version 13.1 documents automated recovery of a whole Active Directory forest from domain-controller backups on vSphere and Hyper-V, and backup and restore of Microsoft Entra ID users, groups, roles, applications and conditional access policies. Other identity providers such as Okta are not mentioned in the pages read.

support.note: The Network Map page describes an interactive view of asset-to-asset and identity-to-asset communication. Help Net Security reported in March 2026 that version 2.0 maps on-premises, cloud, IoT/OT and Kubernetes traffic in one view. The pages describe communication between assets rather than a named application view.

Exhibit A of the Service Agreement says the product learns traffic, creates rules and centrally manages the host operating-system firewalls of all assets. The vendor's pages say only necessary traffic is allowed.

Pages describe on-premises and cloud assets, servers and client devices, OT and IoT devices, and Kubernetes (an eBPF-based pod on each node with enforcement through eBPF and native network policies). Supported operating-system versions and cloud platforms are not listed on the pages read.

The vendor says no software is installed on protected assets: policy is applied through native operating-system firewall components, and through access-control lists on the switches connecting OT devices. No list of supported legacy operating systems was found, and the integrations page marks some switch vendors and OT asset-management integrations as coming soon.
The vendor describes a learning period of 30 days and a simulation mode that shows what a policy would change before it is enforced; Help Net Security reported the same for Network Map 2.0.

The product page says breaches can be contained immediately, and the Network Map is described as showing blast radius and lateral movement paths to speed quarantine. How an asset is isolated was not described on the pages read.

The product page describes automated tagging, grouping and policy creation, and the Kubernetes page shows policy by label. The vendor presents this as removing manual labelling; the policy model itself is not described in detail on the public pages.

support.note: Documented limits include vectors of up to 32,768 dimensions, up to 2,048 compute units per Dedicated cluster in the console and up to 100 replicas. The vendor's home page claims designs for more than 100 billion entities; that figure is a marketing statement.
A built-in BM25 function generates sparse vectors from text; dense and sparse requests are combined in one hybrid search and merged with a reciprocal-rank-fusion or weighted ranker.

Role-based access control works at organisation, project and cluster level, and cluster roles can be limited to specific databases or collections. No row-level or partition-level control is described. The partition-key feature for multi-tenant collections is documented as logical isolation applied through a query filter, not as an enforced access control. Single sign-on and SCIM group sync require the Enterprise plan or BYOC. The open-source project published several advisories in 2025 and 2026 about bypasses of authentication and collection-level access control in Milvus.

Open-source Milvus can be run by the customer on a single machine or as a distributed Kubernetes deployment. Zilliz Cloud BYOC runs the data plane in the customer's cloud account; in the standard BYOC model Zilliz manages it through a cross-account role, and in BYOC-I the customer deploys an agent and keeps control of the infrastructure.

Milvus is licensed under Apache 2.0 and is a graduated project of the LF AI & Data Foundation (graduated June 2021). The vendor states that Zilliz Cloud uses its own engine on top of Milvus; the managed service itself is not open source.

Customer-managed keys are available only in Business Critical projects. The documentation names AWS KMS and Google Cloud KMS and says the feature is not available on Azure, and in one place says it is currently available only in AWS regions; a vendor blog post also names Azure Key Vault. The sources conflict, so coverage by cloud should be confirmed.

customerManagedKeys.note: Business Critical projects only. The customer's KMS key is the root of a key hierarchy covering object storage, local disk and message-queue data. encryption.value: Data at rest is encrypted by default with AES-256, and data in transit with TLS 1.2 or later. The Business Critical plan adds what the vendor calls full-path encryption in transit.

logging.value: Cluster audit logs record data-plane operations including searches, queries and changes to collections, indexes and data. They are delivered to the customer's Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob Storage, or to an HTTPS endpoint, in JSON, ECS or OpenTelemetry format. They require a Dedicated cluster on the Enterprise plan or higher, cannot be enabled together with access logs on the same cluster, and are billed. On BYOC they are written to the data plane's object storage and must be enabled by Zilliz support.

siemIntegration.value: No SIEM product is named in the documentation read. Audit logs can be sent to a generic HTTPS endpoint or to object storage in ECS, OpenTelemetry or JSON format, from which a bank's SIEM could collect them; the Datadog integration carries metrics only.

telemetryExport.value: Cluster metrics can be pushed to Datadog at one-minute frequency or scraped from a Prometheus-format HTTPS endpoint (minimum interval 60 seconds); both are limited to Dedicated clusters in Enterprise projects. independentTests.result: NSS Labs tested Zscaler Zero Trust Exchange alone, in its recommended configuration, and reported overall security effectiveness of 98.85%: exploit block rate 99.05% of 317 exploits, malware block rate 98.65% (4,807 of 4,873), 100% resistance to 583 evasions, 100% on handcrafted malware, and false positive accuracy of 99.63% (15 of 4,098 legitimate samples blocked). No rating tier or comparison with other vendors is given, and the tester does not say who paid. The post's exploit count (311 of 317) does not match its stated percentage.

auditorEvidence.value: The vendor's compliance portal lists audit reports and certificates (including SOC 2 Type 2 and ISO/IEC 27001) and penetration-test report requests, behind access-request buttons. The documents themselves were not reviewed.

logging.value: Transaction logs are held in the Zscaler Nanolog. Nanolog Streaming Service (NSS) streams all logs to the customer's SIEM, either from a virtual machine in the customer's network over TCP or HTTP, or cloud-to-cloud over an HTTPS API feed (Cloud NSS).

siemIntegration.value: NSS is documented as the route for streaming logs to a customer's SIEM for alerting, correlation and long-term archival; the page reviewed does not name specific SIEM products.

telemetryExport.value: Log streaming to external systems through VM-based NSS (raw TCP or HTTP) and Cloud NSS (HTTPS API push).

cloudProviders.note: The service runs mainly in Zscaler's own co-located data centres. AWS and Azure host certain ZIA and ZPA features; Alibaba Cloud is optional, for users in China.

Only the most recent entries for one cloud were reviewed.

regulatoryMappings.statement: Supports the bank in considering how a cloud-delivered zero-trust service relates to DORA's ICT risk and third-party pillars; the vendor's 2024 post is general and does not map products to articles or set out contract terms.

opportunities.point: Expansion into AI security and security operations through acquisitions completed in fiscal 2026 (Red Canary, SPLXAI, SquareX, Symmetry Systems).

strengths.point: Scale: the vendor reports more than 200 data centres and over 750 billion transactions processed daily, with about 11,000 customers.
Published availability commitment of 99.999% for ZIA, ZPA and Zero Trust Branch, with service credits.
Broad list of third-party attestations, with a CSA STAR Level 2 registry entry.

threats.point: A workforce reduction of about 3% and two senior departures were disclosed in 2026.
The August 2025 Salesloft Drift incident showed exposure through third-party SaaS integrations.

weaknesses.point: Regional restriction of traffic (subclouds) has to be arranged through a support ticket rather than self-service.
Still loss-making on a GAAP basis, with an accumulated deficit of US$1,252.7M.

capability.rationale: Anchor 4: five of six listed capabilities are marked yes on the strength of product documentation, and deepfake and injection detection is partial because it appears only as a mention on a marketing page. Anchor 5 needs confirmation by a source other than the vendor.

No release history or deprecation policy was found in the documentation, so anchor 3 is not fully met. Anchor 4 needs named regulated-industry customers.

observability.rationale: Anchor 2: categorised event logs, an administrator audit category, CSV export and webhook delivery are documented. Anchor 3 needs at least one supported SIEM integration, and none was found.

scalability.rationale: Anchor 3: a 99.5% annual uptime SLA, OAuth 2.0 and SAML 2.0 identity providers, sizing guides for self-hosted deployment and a choice of three cloud regions are documented. standards_alignment.rationale: Anchor 2: one attestation is confirmed to cover the product (a SOC 2 Type II report naming Vantage for April 2025 to March 2026). ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification is stated but its scope is not public, so anchor 3 is not fully met.

viability.rationale: Anchor 3 on vendor claims: the company states over 35 years of operation and more than 10,000 customers and is controlled by a private equity firm; no distress signal was found. capability.rationale: Anchor 3: vendor material covers five of six listed capabilities. Domain authentication management is absent, so the coverage test for anchor 4 is not met.

observability.rationale: Anchor 2: a message-level Threat Log, logged remediation actions, per-detection explanations and named SIEM integrations (Splunk, QRadar) are described, but a documented audit trail of administrator actions and its export, which anchor 3 requires, were not found in public pages.

risk_country.rationale: Anchor 3: US headquarters and lead investors are disclosed, and hosting (US or EU) and support locations are listed. scalability.rationale: Anchor 3: two signals are evidenced. standards_alignment.rationale: Anchor 2: one current third-party attestation is registry-confirmed and covers the product in its government edition: the FedRAMP Marketplace lists 'Abnormal AI for Government' as FedRAMP Certified (Class C, Moderate, since 2025-04-11). The offering is named after the vendor rather than the product; it is counted because Abnormal Email Security is the vendor's single main offering in this dataset, with the caveat that the listing covers the government deployment, not the commercial service. The vendor also states SOC 2 Type II and ISO/IEC 27001, 27701 and 42001 certification, each with scope not published, and a CSA STAR listing with no level stated. viability.rationale: Anchor 3: US$546 million raised, the last round in August 2024 at a reported US$5.1 billion valuation, with a company-claimed annual recurring revenue above US$200 million; no distress signals met the evidence bar. capability.rationale: Anchor 2: the product delivers the core function of secure remote access to applications, and the vendor's product pages describe zero-trust network access, a secure web gateway and an in-line cloud access security broker. Of the six listed capabilities, branch networking is outside the product's scope, inspection of encrypted traffic was not found, and regional processing choice is shown only for customer-hosted servers, so several are partial or absent. Anchor 3 needs most listed capabilities covered.

maturity.rationale: Anchor 4: generally available for more than three years (a customer story dates use to 2012, and a 2021 securities filing records Absolute's purchase of NetMotion, the product's origin), with named regulated-industry customers in vendor customer stories: Lincoln International, the UK insurance broker Alan Boswell Group and Finanz Informatik, the IT provider of the German savings banks. The vendor publishes dated advisories per release and states that it supports the current and previous major versions with 12 months' notice of end of life. Anchor 5 needs regulated customers in production confirmed by a source other than the vendor, and none was found.

risk_country.rationale: Anchor 3, the same as the vendor's other product: ownership is disclosed and a sub-processor list by country is published. Sanctions screening has not been run.

scalability.rationale: Anchor 3: at least two of the five are evidenced. Anchor 4 needs adoption at large-enterprise scale shown in documentation, a filing or independent press: the largest documented deployments read are about 10,000 and 6,300 users, and the hosted service's regions were not found.

standards_alignment.rationale: Anchor 2: one current third-party attestation. The vendor states that the Secure Access Cloud service has a SOC 2 Type 2 report, which is not public. The vendor's ISO/IEC 27001 certificate names Secure Endpoint as the only product in scope and the FedRAMP Marketplace entry read covers the Secure Endpoint suite, so neither counts here. viability.rationale: Anchor 3: revenue-backed with no distress signal found. The company was bought for an enterprise value of about US$870 million in 2023 as reported by SecurityWeek, has since made two acquisitions (2024 and 2026), and states that thousands of enterprises are customers. The only staff reduction found was about 5% in April 2023. capability.rationale: Anchor 4: six of the seven listed capabilities are shown in specific vendor material, namely the published features matrix, the public API documentation and release notes (inventory, patching, software deployment, remote freeze, wipe and location, self-healing and scripted remediation, and remote recovery through Rehydrate playbooks); configuration policy is partial because compliance policies assess and report device state but general configuration management is not described. Patching and workflow automation need the top editions and firmware-level actions need eligible Windows devices. Anchor 5 needs confirmation by a source other than the vendor, such as an independent test or a deployment published by a regulated customer, and none was found.

maturity.rationale: Anchor 4: the product has been generally available for well over three years (a customer story dates one deployment to 2014, and SecurityWeek described the firmware-embedded product in 2023), with named regulated-industry customers in vendor customer stories: Allina Health with about 10,000 devices, Apria Healthcare and the Royal Free London NHS trust. Release notes are published per version. The remote recovery feature dates from September 2025 and Linux support from November 2026. Anchor 5 needs bank or comparable regulated customers confirmed by a source other than the vendor and a published support and deprecation policy; the FedRAMP Marketplace shows five authorisation letters but does not name the agencies, and no lifecycle policy for this product was found.

observability.rationale: Anchor 3: the console help documents an event history that records administrative changes with the acting user and old and new values, behind its own audit permission; events can be exported from the console and through a documented API; and a SIEM Connector forwards events by syslog, an integration that Google also documents with its own parser. Anchor 4 needs configurable retention and tamper-evident audit records: retention is fixed at 30, 90 or 365 days by event type and no tamper protection is described.

risk_country.rationale: Anchor 3: ownership is disclosed (wholly owned by the US private equity firm Crosspoint Capital Partners; Canadian and US operating companies), and the vendor publishes its sub-processors by country and its data-centre regions in the United States, Canada, the European Union, the United Kingdom and India. Anchor 4 is not claimed because the pages read do not say that the customer chooses the region, and the locations of support staff were not found. Sanctions screening has not been run.

scalability.rationale: Anchor 3: at least two of the five are evidenced. The features matrix lists single sign-on, two-factor authentication and role-based access control; the service runs from data centres in five regions plus a US federal instance; and the public API documents request limits (up to 10,000 devices per freeze request). Anchor 4 needs adoption at large-enterprise scale shown in documentation, a filing or independent press: the largest documented deployments read are about 10,000 and 7,000 devices, the vendor's figure of 600 million devices counts firmware shipped and not devices under management, and no availability commitment is published.

standards_alignment.rationale: Anchor 3: two current third-party attestations cover the product. The ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certificate (Baker Tilly Certifications ISO20250201, to 2029-04-26) names Secure Endpoint as the product in scope, and the FedRAMP Marketplace lists the Absolute Secure Endpoint Product Suite as certified at Moderate since 2025-03-04, the US federal instance of the product. The basis is vendor-documented because the ISO certificate was read from the vendor's copy and not confirmed in the certifier's directory. viability.rationale: Anchor 3: revenue-backed with no distress signal found. capability.rationale: Anchor 3: covers most listed capabilities. The vendor's product pages and datasheet describe all seven: network and system decoys, endpoint breadcrumbs and baits, fake accounts and credentials in identity stores, cloud honeytokens, automated design of deception, mapping of intruder activity to MITRE ATT&CK, and integrations for alerting and response. Anchor 4 is not met because this rests on marketing pages and a two-page datasheet; the technical documentation is behind the support portal and was not read. A US Navy announcement confirms that Acalvio's technology won first place in a 2025 challenge judged on usability, features and technical performance, but it does not name the product or publish results, so it does not confirm the listed capabilities.

maturity.rationale: Anchor 3: named production customers and a regular release history. ShadowPlex has been generally available since April 2017, which is more than three years. Production use is named by Broadcom and ABP Group in quotes carried in the vendor's own datasheet and release, and Honeywell built a product on it in 2022; the vendor announced platform additions in March, July and September 2026. Anchor 4 is not met: no regulated-industry customer is named (the financial services references are anonymous) and no customer numbers are disclosed.

observability.rationale: Anchor 3, at low confidence: the vendor names SIEM integrations (Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, ArcSight, NetWitness, Securonix), describes alert delivery to SIEM and SOAR tools and by webhook, and its Data Processing Addendum says administrative access to the service is logged and logs are protected from change. These are general statements; no documentation of the audit trail a customer can see, or of an export interface, was read. Anchor 4 is not met: configurable retention and tamper-evident audit records available to the customer are not described.

standards_alignment.rationale: Anchor 2: one third-party attestation with scope unclear. scalability.rationale: Anchor 2: one of the five is evidenced, enterprise identity integration, from the platform's listed SAML and OIDC single sign-on and SCIM provisioning; the product is also described as deployable silently through device management tools. Anchor 4 is not met: retention settings and tamper-evident records are not documented, and the trail does not visibly cover sign-ins or administrator access.

risk_country.rationale: Anchor 4: the company is a Belgian private company in the public register with its lead investors named in the press, and the documentation gives separate EU, US and Australian instances with data stored in-region, so a customer can choose a processing region among the covered jurisdictions. SAML single sign-on and role and team permissions are documented. Anchor 5 needs a regulated-enterprise deployment confirmed by a source other than the vendor, or independently published performance; neither was found.

ISO/IEC 42001 is described with a scope naming the platform's AI features, and the government edition runs inside a host's FedRAMP Moderate authorisation, which counts once as held by a host; the FedRAMP data file confirms the host's authorisation but does not name Aikido. capability.rationale: Anchor 4: six of the seven listed capabilities are covered and one is partial, shown in Fastly's published product terms. maturity.rationale: Anchor 4. observability.rationale: Anchor 3: Fastly's documentation describes corp, site and account audit logs, an API feed for bulk export of stored request data, and alert integrations with Datadog and Sumo Logic, with the feed described as the route into SIEM tools. risk_country.rationale: Anchor 3: ownership is disclosed in securities filings (Nasdaq-listed, headquartered in San Francisco, with three institutional holders above 5% and no controlling shareholder), and Fastly publishes its sub-processors and affiliates by country, including the countries where Amazon Web Services and MongoDB Atlas process Next-Gen WAF data. standards_alignment.rationale: Anchor 2. Fastly's compliance page lists three current third-party attestations: PCI DSS Level 1 Service Provider, ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and SOC 2 Type 2. The ISO and SOC 2 entries are statements about the company with no scope given, and the certifier's directory entry for the ISO certificate could not be read, so anchor 3 (two or more attestations whose scope covers the product) is not fully met. The score may rise once the certificate scope and the SOC 2 report are seen; see the gap on attestation scope. One PCI DSS control mapping is published for the client-side add-on.

viability.rationale: Anchor 4: a listed company with audited financials, 2025 revenue of US$624.0 million (up 15%), US$365.2 million of cash and marketable securities at 30 September 2026, positive operating cash flow (US$94.4 million in 2025 and US$108.2 million in the first nine months of 2026) and an undrawn US$100 million credit facility. The exposure test in rubric 0.4.1 does not bind: borrowings of US$330 million in convertible notes are below annual revenue, and the pending securities class action seeks unspecified damages with no judgment.
